1976-the-swine-flu-programme-that-was-st.context_blurb:
In 1976 the United States set out to vaccinate everyone against a flu that never came. Three things in the story were true at once: the official forecast was wrong, the safety monitoring caught a real but rare harm, and the government listened to its own data and stopped.

It began in February 1976 with one death. Private David Lewis, a young recruit at Fort Dix in New Jersey, rose from his sickbed for a forced night march, collapsed and died. The CDC grew a swine flu from his body that looked like a near relative of the 1918 virus, which had killed some fifty million people worldwide. That resemblance alone turned one barracks death into a national campaign.

Gerald Ford, the president, went on television beside Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin to urge every citizen to get the shot, and some 45 million Americans did so within about ten weeks. Yet when flu season ended, the Fort Dix strain had not turned up even once anywhere else on Earth. The forecast pandemic simply never arrived.

Meanwhile the CDC's monitoring had found more cases than normal of Guillain-Barré syndrome, a creeping paralysis, at about one additional case for every hundred thousand doses. On 16 December the government suspended the campaign across the whole nation. It was never restarted at scale. A missed forecast, a harm caught and a programme halted on its own evidence: that is what a working safety system looks like.

1986-what-happens-when-you-take-away-the.context_blurb:
Since 1988 an American family convinced that a vaccine harmed a child cannot simply sue the maker. It must go instead to a special federal vaccine court created by a 1986 law. How that law came about is a story of lawsuits, a vanishing vaccine supply and an argument still going on.

The idea had a rehearsal in 1976. During the swine flu campaign the Federal Insurance Company warned Merck that it would drop the firm's lawsuit cover, and no maker would ship a dose unprotected. So that August Congress made the federal government itself answer for injury claims. In 1986 the arrangement became permanent.

Then the lawsuits multiplied. From 1978 to 1981 just nine families sued over DTP, the baby shot against whooping cough, diphtheria and tetanus. Once lawyers began arguing that a maker could owe damages even when nobody had been careless, the count rose past two hundred suits a year by the mid-1980s. Insurers walked away or demanded premiums the makers could not pay, and company after company quit. By the mid-1980s only one American firm still made the DTP shot that every child was meant to get.

Ronald Reagan signed the new act in November 1986, but his written statement said he had serious doubts and approved it reluctantly. He objected that judges, not the executive branch, would run the payouts, and the court did not open until October 1988.

The makers do not pay the awards. An excise tax on every dose sold in America fills a federal trust fund, so the vaccinated in effect finance their own compensation. The tax is not one flat price; it rises with the number of diseases a vaccine prevents. A flu shot against one disease pays 75 cents, while measles-mumps-rubella, against three, pays $2.25.

No jury sits in this court. A judge-like official called a special master hears each claim, the health secretary is the formal opponent, and the lawyers arguing against the family come from the Department of Justice. The company that made the vaccine is not in the room.

A family still needs a lawyer, but Congress banned the usual deal: no cut of the award and no other fee from the family. Instead the programme pays reasonable legal fees whether the family wins or loses, provided the claim was brought in good faith with a reasonable basis. A winning family gets its medical bills and lost earnings paid without limit. Only pain and suffering and the death benefit for a child who dies are capped, both at $250,000, a figure set in 1986 and never raised for inflation.

By September 2025 the programme had paid 12,339 of 28,991 petitions, about $5.4 billion in all. HRSA, the agency in charge, adds a qualifier: roughly 60 percent of the money came through negotiated settlements in which the health department never concluded from the evidence that the vaccine caused the injury.

Ordinary courts were not completely shut. Hannah Bruesewitz developed a seizure disorder after a DTP shot as a baby, and her parents took the maker, Wyeth, to court rather than accept the vaccine court's decision. The Supreme Court decided against them in February 2011 by six votes to two. Writing for the majority, Justice Antonin Scalia shut American courtrooms to one argument: that the vaccine could have been made to a safer design. If a vaccine was properly made and properly labelled, he reasoned, its remaining side effects counted as unavoidable.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, dissented. The majority's reading, she warned, left a regulatory vacuum in which no one makes sure vaccine makers keep pace with scientific advances. Supporters of the shield reply that it kept makers in business and gives families a cheaper, faster hearing than a jury trial.

A section of the 1986 Act headed "Mandate for safer childhood vaccines" orders the health secretary to push for vaccines with fewer and milder reactions and to report progress to Congress. In 2017 the Informed Consent Action Network filed a freedom-of-information request for those reports and sued the next year. The department answered in court that its searches had found no such records. That is a no-records-found reply, not a confession; the group's stronger claim, that no report was ever filed, is its own. The lawyer who signed the suit, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., was by 2025 the health secretary himself.

1998-the-expansion-that-refused-to-slow-.context_blurb:
For most of the twentieth century astronomers assumed that the universe, flung outward by the Big Bang, must be slowing as the gravity of everything in it pulls back. In 1998 two rival teams set out to measure that braking and found the opposite, a discovery that won Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Measuring vast distances takes a "standard candle", a light whose true brightness you know. Both teams used Type Ia supernovae. Each starts as a white dwarf, the Earth-sized leftover of a star, which steals matter from a companion until it nears the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4 times the Sun's mass. At that threshold it reignites in runaway fusion and blows apart, and because the trigger is the same everywhere, every blast peaks at nearly the same true brightness.

Perlmutter's team worked from Berkeley and Schmidt's from Australia, and both built their surveys to pin down one number: how hard gravity was braking the cosmic expansion.

Instead, their distant supernovae came out about 10 to 15 percent dimmer than a slowing universe allows. Dimmer means farther: the light had travelled longer than gravity alone could explain, so space had been stretching faster over time. The expansion of the universe is not slowing; it is speeding up.

Riess and his High-z teammates did not celebrate. For years they tried to destroy their own result, testing the two respectable ways to dim far-off supernovae without any speed-up: a fine grey dust drifting between galaxies, and the chance that supernovae in the young universe were born fainter. Neither effect proved big enough, and two hostile teams reaching the same unwanted answer is why the world believed it.

Nobody knew what was pushing. Michael Turner, a University of Chicago cosmologist, chose a name in 1998 that assumed nothing: "dark energy", dark because no one can see it and energy because it was the most general word he could find.

In the equations, the simplest stand-in for it is an old idea: Einstein's cosmological constant, written with the Greek letter Lambda. Einstein added it in 1917 to hold the universe still, then dropped it once Edwin Hubble showed space expanding. The tale that he called it his biggest blunder comes secondhand, from George Gamow, and may never have been said.

A tempting guess is that empty space carries a quantum energy of its own. But when physicists calculate how much and compare it with what the sky shows, the prediction overshoots by about 120 orders of magnitude, a factor of 1 followed by 120 zeros. Even a gentler cutoff leaves a gap of around 56, the worst mismatch between theory and measurement in physics. It is called the vacuum catastrophe, and what dark energy really is remains unknown.

51-pegasi-b-and-the-dip-a-backyard-can-m.context_blurb:
Until 1995 nobody knew whether stars like the Sun had planets. That October Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, two astronomers from Switzerland, announced one circling 51 Pegasi, an ordinary star some fifty light years away. Their ELODIE spectrograph in southern France had caught the star wobbling as an unseen planet tugged it to and fro. The planet, 51 Pegasi b, was a Jupiter-sized giant racing round its star every four days.

Other teams already had instruments sharp enough to find it. They missed it because theory said giant planets need orbits lasting years, so they checked each star only now and then, far too slowly to catch a wobble that repeats every four days. Their old data, rechecked after 1995, held the signal all along.

Nor was it the very first world beyond the Sun. In 1992 Aleksander Wolszczan and his colleague Dale Frail, listening with the giant Arecibo dish, had found two planets around a millisecond pulsar, a star spinning hundreds of times a second. Its pulses tick like a metronome, and the planets' tugs nudged the timing.

The wobble gives only a planet's minimum mass, because the tilt of the orbit is hidden. A transit fills the gap: when a planet crosses its star's face, the depth of the dip in starlight reveals the planet's radius. Radius plus mass gives density, which tells rock from gas. A dip of about one percent is big enough for a patient amateur with a good camera and a tracking mount to record.

A transit can even sample a planet's air, as a thin ring of starlight shines through its atmosphere. In 2002 David Charbonneau's team, watching HD 209458 b with the Hubble Space Telescope, caught the yellow signature of sodium in its air, the first atmosphere ever detected on a planet outside our Solar System.

a-nail-a-wire-and-a-battery-the-electrom.context_blurb:
An electromagnet is iron that grips while current flows through a coil around it and lets go the instant the current stops. An English shoemaker turned scientist, William Sturgeon, and an American schoolteacher, Joseph Henry, built the first strong ones, and their on-off trick ended up inside the telegraph and, later, the computer.

In 1825 Sturgeon bent soft iron into a horseshoe, wrapped it in bare copper wire and wired it to a single battery cell. The magnet weighed about as much as a pocket watch, yet it lifted nine pounds, some twenty times its own weight, and dropped the load the moment the circuit broke. Insulated wire did not exist yet, so to stop the current leaking through the core, Sturgeon painted the iron itself with varnish. The bare loops still could not touch, so they lay in one loose layer, which capped the number of turns.

Try it on a kitchen table. Coil wire around a steel nail, touch the ends to an AA battery and count the paperclips it lifts; add ten more turns and count again. The count usually goes up, because strength grows with the number of turns times the current. Keep each touch brief: a battery wired straight across heats up fast.

Joseph Henry, at the Albany Academy in New York, broke Sturgeon's limit around 1830 by wrapping each strand of wire in silk, so that hundreds of turns could be stacked tight on one core. Family legend says his wife Harriet gave up strips of her petticoat. In 1831 his record magnet for Yale College held up 2,063 pounds, a little over a ton.

That year Henry also strung a wire roughly a mile long around a lecture room at the Academy, with a battery at one end and a magnet at the other. Whenever he completed the circuit, the far magnet jumped and struck a bell: a weak current doing work at a distance. It was the telegraph's principle, five years before Samuel Morse patented his.

Morse's long lines faded over the miles until the current was too weak to work anything. Henry's relay fixed that. Placed every few miles, it let the faint current energise a small coil that pulled an iron lever, and the lever closed a second circuit with a fresh local battery, sending a full-strength copy down the next stretch. Soft iron lets go instantly, so the lever snapped back cleanly every time; relays are the ancestors of every switch in a computer.

a-sheep-a-duck-and-a-rooster-fly-first.context_blurb:
In 1783 people left the ground for the first time in history, and France was where it happened. Two rival kinds of balloon rose that year: the hot-air balloons of the Montgolfier brothers, paper makers from the town of Annonay, and the hydrogen balloons of the Parisian scientist Jacques Charles.

The first passengers of all were farm animals. On 19 September 1783, before King Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette and a crowd of tens of thousands at Versailles, a Montgolfier balloon carried a duck, a rooster and a sheep into the sky. Eight minutes and about three kilometres later, all three came down alive. The sheep even had a name, Montauciel, which means "Climb-to-the-sky". The rooster's hurt wing came from a kick by the sheep, not from the flight.

The crew was chosen like a small experiment with comparisons built in. The duck was already known to cope with height, and the rooster was a bird that never flies high. The sheep, big-bodied, with a heart and circulation thought closest to ours, went up as a living stand-in for a human passenger.

The Montgolfiers had the right machine for the wrong reason. They lit fires of wet wool and straw under the bag's open mouth, convinced that the smoke itself did the lifting, and even named the imaginary lifting stuff "Montgolfier gas". The true cause is density. Heating air spreads its molecules apart, so the warm air inside weighs less than the same volume of cool air outside, and the heavier outside air pushes the balloon up.

Charles had already flown the other kind. On 27 August 1783 his unmanned hydrogen balloon, Le Globe, rose silently over Paris from the Champ-de-Mars and drifted for miles before settling near the village of Gonesse. The farmers there took it for a monster dropped from the sky and ripped it to pieces with pitchforks and knives.

People followed within weeks. On 21 November 1783 Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes rode a Montgolfier balloon some nine kilometres across Paris in about twenty-five minutes, the first free flight any human being had ever made. Louis XVI had suggested sending condemned prisoners, but Pilâtre de Rozier argued that the honour belonged to free men.

On 1 December 1783 Charles flew a hydrogen balloon himself, from the Tuileries, with his partner Nicolas-Louis Robert. After Robert climbed out, the lightened balloon carried Charles alone up to about three thousand metres, where his ears hurt so badly that he could not bear the thought of a second time, and he never flew again. High up the outside air is thin, and the denser air trapped behind each eardrum pushes outward against it.

The two designs were steered in different ways. A hot-air pilot climbed by feeding the fire and came down by opening a vent at the top. A hydrogen balloon has no fire: once its gas is sealed in, the only way to make it rise is to throw weight over the side, which is why its pilots carried sacks of ballast to drop. Letting gas out is how it comes down.

abbes-wall-the-limit-that-had-to-be-dodg.context_blurb:
For two centuries, seeing smaller things meant grinding better lenses. Then Ernst Abbe, a German physicist, proved in 1873 that past a certain point no glass could help. Light is a wave, so two points nearer each other than roughly half its wavelength smear into one, however perfect the lens.

Visible light runs from about 400 nanometres for violet to 700 for red, so Abbe's wall stands at roughly 200 nanometres, about the size of the smallest bacterium. Below that line things were not merely fuzzy; they were invisible. A ribosome, about 25 nanometres across, a virus, at 20 to 100, and the gap between two nerve cells, at 50 to 100, all stayed hidden behind the wall for some sixty years.

The first way around it was to stop using light. Electrons, treated as waves, have wavelengths thousands of times shorter than visible light. Ernst Ruska, working with his teacher Max Knoll, built the first electron lens in 1931, and by September 1933 his electron microscope magnified 12,000 times, finer than any light microscope could manage.

Others kept ordinary light and outwitted the wall. Stefan Hell's 1999 method, called STED, surrounds the glowing spot in a fluorescence microscope with a second beam shaped like a doughnut. The doughnut switches off the glow everywhere except its tiny dark centre, so only molecules there can shine. Newspapers reported that the limit had been broken, but the Nobel committee put it more carefully: the limit still stands, and Hell had shrunk the region allowed to give off light.

Eric Betzig attacked from the other side. In PALM, the method he and Harald Hess showed in 2006, a single molecule lights up at a time. On the camera it still shows as a fat blur some 250 nanometres across, but a blur from one source has a centre, and Betzig computed that centre to within a few nanometres, then repeated the trick with the next lone molecule, thousands of times over. The dots add up to a picture no lens could form. In 2014 Hell, Betzig and William Moerner shared a Nobel Prize.

aktion-t4-and-the-american-pedigree.context_blurb:
Between 1939 and 1945 doctors in Nazi Germany murdered disabled people by the tens of thousands, in a programme later called Aktion T4. It belongs to the history of science because it grew out of eugenics, the theory, taught in leading universities, that a nation could breed itself better by stopping the "unfit" from having children, and that theory had deep American roots.

The first step was sterilization. Within months of taking power, the Nazi government passed its sterilization law of July 1933, in force from January 1934. To issue the orders it created a new network of Erbgesundheitsgerichte, Genetic Health Courts, in districts across Germany, with the power to sterilize by force. About 360,000 people had been sterilized by 1939 and some 400,000 by 1945.

Its authors had a model. The German law closely followed the Model Eugenical Sterilization Law drafted by the American Harry Laughlin, who ran the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor on Carnegie and Rockefeller money. In 1936 the University of Heidelberg gave Laughlin an honorary doctorate for his work.

The killing came next, and it never rested on a law. In October 1939 Hitler put his signature to a brief private letter on his own stationery and dated it back to 1 September 1939, the day the war began. Doctors had refused to kill without written cover, and this page gave it to them. It put two men in charge: Philipp Bouhler, head of Hitler's Chancellery, and Karl Brandt, his personal physician. Brandt was later hanged after the Nuremberg Doctors' Trial.

The programme was run from a villa in Berlin at Tiergartenstrasse 4, and that street address gave it the name insiders used: T4. On paper it hid behind a harmless-sounding charity. Its first victims were disabled people, Germans in hospitals and asylums, gassed with carbon monoxide at six killing centres, some of them in old castles. Those rooms were in use before the Holocaust's death camps existed.

The halt came from a pulpit. On 3 August 1941, in his cathedral at Münster, Bishop Clemens August von Galen condemned the killings in public. Copies of the sermon passed from hand to hand, and British planes later dropped it as leaflets. Hitler judged an open clash with the Catholic Church too costly and left Galen free, though priests who read the sermon aloud were persecuted. On 24 August Hitler ordered the centralized gassing stopped. An honest account adds a second fact: the T4 office had also just reached its own projected quota of deaths. The sermon was the most effective public protest against any Nazi policy, but one sermon alone did not end the killing.

Hospital doctors and nurses went on murdering patients until 1945, now by lethal injection and deliberate starvation, a phase the T4 apparatus itself called Wilde Euthanasie, "wild euthanasia". Counting it, estimates of the dead across Germany, Austria and occupied Europe reach 250,000 to 300,000.

The killers kept careful books. In June 1945 Charles Dameron, an American investigator, forced a safe at Hartheim, one of the killing centres, and found a 39-page brochure from the T4 office. Its figure of 70,273 was the number of people gassed, tallied month by month across the six centres. The same brochure worked out the "savings" in food and care that the deaths had brought: a horror run as administration.

After the war Leo Alexander, an American army psychiatrist who had gathered evidence against the Nazi doctors at Nuremberg, warned his own profession. In a 1949 article for American physicians, "Medical Science under Dictatorship", he traced it all back to a small shift among doctors: accepting the idea that some lives are not worth living. Everything else, he argued, followed from that one premise.

all-cells-from-cells-and-the-man-who-got.context_blurb:
Every living thing, from an oak to a frog to you, is built of cells, and every cell is born from an older one. Both halves of that idea were won in Germany between 1837 and 1858. The men who got the first half right got the second half wrong, and the man who fixed it got almost no credit.

Matthias Schleiden came to science late. He trained in law, qualifying in 1827, and set up in Hamburg as a courtroom advocate, but the practice failed, he sank into depression, and he turned to botany. In Berlin in 1837 he was at dinner with Theodor Schwann, telling him about the little bodies he kept finding in every plant. Schwann had met the same little bodies in animal tissue, so the two got up from the meal and went straight to a microscope to compare. Schleiden published the claim for plants in 1838, and Schwann extended it to animals in 1839. The dinner is documented; the neat quotation pinned to it is a later retelling.

One part of the cell already had a name. In 1831 the Scottish botanist Robert Brown peeled an orchid and saw one dark spot in cell after cell. He called it the nucleus, the name it still carries, and told the Linnean Society nothing about its job: he left that question open.

Schleiden and Schwann were right that plants and animals alike are made of cells, but wrong about where new ones come from, because neither thought an existing cell played any part. They pictured a new cell forming the way a crystal grows in syrup, condensing out of a shapeless fluid in the tissue. Schleiden even named the fluid, cytoblastema, and wrote out its ingredients like a cook: sugar, gum and mucus.

The correction came from Berlin. In 1852 the anatomist Robert Remak watched animal cells pinch themselves in two, showing that new cells come from division. Then in April 1855 Rudolf Virchow printed the Latin slogan omnis cellula a cellula, meaning that every cell comes from a cell, in a medical journal, the Archiv, which he himself had founded and edited.

Remak and Virchow had joined the Berlin faculty in the same year, 1847, and worked in the same laboratory. Remak's evidence won few converts until Virchow pushed the idea hard, yet Virchow himself had at first doubted the evidence that cells divide. Remak's road was steeper. Prussian law kept Jews out of university teaching, the king refused him in 1843, and only after years of pressure from Alexander von Humboldt did a royal order in 1847 make Remak the first Jew allowed to lecture at the University of Berlin while keeping his religion. The post came with no salary and no laboratory, so he paid for his research out of his medical practice.

Virchow's 1855 essay never cited Remak. When Remak wrote to point out how close it was to his own 1852 work, Virchow brushed him off, and in the preface to an 1858 book he explained that no citation had been owed because the 1855 piece was only an editorial, not a scientific paper. The historian Paul Weindling calls it plagiarism; that is his judgment, not a court's. Remak lost the Berlin chair of pathology to Virchow in 1856, never became a full professor and died suddenly at fifty.

Every cell in you sits at the end of an unbroken chain of divisions. Ron Milo, Ron Sender and Shai Fuchs published a careful count in 2016: about 30 trillion cells in a human body, and roughly nine in ten of them belong to the blood-forming lineage, because blood cells are tiny and enormously numerous.

Yet the chain needs a first link, a cell formed from lifeless chemistry. In 1952 Miller and Urey sent sparks through hydrogen, methane and ammonia and made amino acids. The experiment works and has been repeated; the trouble is the recipe. Earth's early air was probably not that strongly reducing mixture but something closer to neutral, which would have made far fewer amino acids. And amino acids are a long way from a cell. No one yet knows how life began.

aluminium-from-an-emperors-cutlery-to-a-.context_blurb:
Aluminium is the metal of soda cans and kitchen foil, yet in the 1850s it was, ounce for ounce, the costliest metal on Earth, dearer than gold. Its journey from treasure to throwaway runs through a stubborn chemical bond, an emperor's money and two young inventors who found the same trick in the same year.

Emperor Napoleon III of France is said to have saved aluminium forks and knives for his most honoured dinner guests, while lesser guests made do with gold and silver. The tale is not documented, but the price was real.

The odd thing is that aluminium is not rare. It is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, outnumbered among all elements only by oxygen and silicon. But it never occurs as metal, because it clings to oxygen so tightly that no furnace fired with wood or charcoal, the kind that had freed iron and copper for thousands of years, can pull the two apart.

Chemists had to free it with other, costly metals. Friedrich Wöhler, a German chemist, isolated aluminium as a fine grey powder in 1827. A year later he did something more famous still: he made urea, a compound until then known only from living bodies, out of ammonium cyanate in a glass flask. That broke the old belief that only living things could make the "organic" molecules of life.

In the 1850s, with Napoleon III paying, Henri Sainte-Claire Deville swapped Wöhler's expensive potassium for cheaper sodium and used it to pull aluminium out of aluminium chloride. At the Paris exhibition of 1855, twelve of his small bars lay beside the French Crown Jewels, labelled "silver from clay". The "clay" was bauxite ore, and the emperor hoped the light metal would one day equip his soldiers.

Thirty years later it was still a jewel. On 6 December 1884 builders capped the Washington Monument with a 100-ounce pyramid of cast aluminium. Before it went up, Tiffany's in New York showed it off for two days, and people later boasted of having stepped over the monument's very tip.

Then in 1886 two 22-year-olds on different continents, Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult in France, found the same trick within months of each other, and it still carries both their names: the Hall-Héroult process. They dissolved alumina in molten cryolite, which lets it melt far below its usual melting point, and passed an electric current through the bath to pull out the metal. Within a generation the price fell about a hundredfold.

Smelting from ore still devours electricity, but melting down old cans and window frames takes only about 5 percent of that energy. Because the metal can be remelted again and again, roughly three quarters of all the aluminium ever made is still at work today.

alvins-lights-on-the-galapagos-rift.context_blurb:
In February 1977 the little American submarine Alvin sank some two and a half kilometres to the floor of the Pacific at the Galapagos Rift, off Ecuador, where the seafloor splits and new crust is born. Its lights found a crowded oasis of life in permanent darkness, and a rule every textbook taught fell apart.

Nobody aboard expected animals. At the controls of dive 713 was Jack Donnelly; beside him sat Jack Corliss, from Oregon State, and Tjeerd van Andel, from Stanford. The whole cruise was staffed by geologists and geochemists who had come for hot springs and fresh lava, and not one biologist was on the expedition.

Around a vent gushing warm, mineral-rich water lay clams the size of dinner plates, white and up to 30 centimetres long, spread over some fifty metres of new lava. The scientists named the spot Clambake 1 over the radio, and the name stuck.

Every biology book of 1977 taught that all food chains begin with sunlight captured by photosynthesis, and here was a thriving community where sunlight never reaches. Its energy came from below. Microbes at the bottom of the food chain there live on hydrogen sulfide, which streams from the vents: they burn it for energy and use that energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide, much as plants use light. This is chemosynthesis. Sergei Winogradsky had described such bacteria in the 1880s; what was new was a whole ecosystem running on them, with no help from the Sun.

The ship was not equipped for biology. When the small supply of formaldehyde ran out with clams and worms still coming up, so the story goes, the crew pickled specimens in Russian vodka bought when the ship passed through Panama. It is a much-retold expedition tale, best treated as legend.

One vent animal made the mystery impossible to ignore: the giant tube worm Riftia pachyptila, which grows as long as three metres and faster than any other known sea invertebrate. Cut open an adult and you find a heart and nerves but no mouth, no gut and no anus. It has no digestive tract at all, so whatever feeds it is never swallowed.

The answer came from a student. At a Harvard seminar in 1980 the biologist Meredith Jones described the mouthless worm and the crystals of pure sulfur found in its body. Colleen Cavanaugh, a first-year graduate student, jumped up and proposed that bacteria living inside the worm were making its food from chemicals in the vent water. Jones handed her a specimen, and in 1981 she led the paper that proved it: billions of sulfur-oxidising bacteria live packed into a spongy organ called the trophosome, which fills most of the worm's trunk. The worm is a farm. Its red plume, rich in haemoglobin, gathers hydrogen sulfide and oxygen from the water and carries them down to its tenants.

The deep had one more surprise. Explorers on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge found the Lost City in December 2000: a field of white carbonate chimneys heated by no volcano at all. There, seawater reacting with mantle rock gives off hydrogen and methane, a process called serpentinization, and the vent fluids are only 40 to 90 degrees Celsius. The tallest chimney rises about 60 metres, as high as a twenty-storey building.

apollo-13-the-failure-that-was-built-in-.context_blurb:
In April 1970, while bound for the Moon, an oxygen tank burst aboard Apollo 13, carrying Jack Swigert, Fred Haise and Jim Lovell. They never landed. Crew and ground team spent four days improvising a way home, and the cause had been built into the ship long before launch.

The rescue route set a record by accident. The wide loop around the Moon's far side carried the three men about 400,171 kilometres from home, farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone, a record that stood until the Artemis II crew passed it on 6 April 2026.

The first sign was a loud bang, 56 hours out. Seconds later Swigert reported trouble and Lovell named it: a sudden drop in voltage on the Main B electrical bus. Out of the window Lovell then watched gas venting away in a white cloud, and the crew's first guess was that a meteoroid had smashed into the ship. The trouble was in fact inside.

Thirty hours into the flight the ship had left its free-return path for a course aimed at the Fra Mauro highlands. On a free return, the Moon's own gravity swings the ship around in a loop and sends it back toward Earth with no further burn. A 34-second burn, the first order from Houston, put the ship back on it. The service module's big engine sat beside the wrecked bay and could not be trusted. So both that burn and a later one of over four minutes, which brought splashdown roughly twelve hours sooner, came from the engine meant to set the lunar module down on the Moon: its descent engine.

The men sheltered in the lunar module, Aquarius. It cleaned its air with round canisters of lithium hydroxide, which soak up carbon dioxide, and with three men breathing they were soon spent. The command module had spares, but they were square, and the lunar module's sockets were round. Engineers led by Ed Smylie had under two days to design an adapter from things already aboard. The capsule communicator, Joe Kerwin, read up the parts list, which included two water-cooled undergarments; Houston wanted only the plastic bags those garments were stowed in. A bypass hole at the centre of each square canister would let air dodge the chemical entirely, so it had to be plugged. The popular telling says a sock went in, but the transcript shows the crew chose a towel.

Near home the approach was too shallow, and a last small correction was needed with the computer powered down. Lovell held the ship's attitude by hand, Haise managed the throttle, and they aimed by the crescent Earth in the window, its lit horn lying on the crosshair of the sight.

The command module, Odyssey, had been shut down cold, and nobody had ever brought one back to life from that state. Ken Mattingly, dropped from the crew just before launch because he had been exposed to rubella, spent under two days in the simulator, working beside the flight controller John Aaron, hunting for an order of switch throws that would not drain the batteries dry.

Oxygen was never the shortage; water was. Aquarius cooled its electronics with a sublimator: water fed into porous plates open to space froze in the pores, and the heat of the electronics turned that ice straight into vapour, which blew away into the vacuum carrying the heat with it. The men cut their own drinking to about a fifth of normal.

The cause had been built in long before. In October 1968 a crew lifting an oxygen shelf out of a service module left one bolt in place, and the shelf dropped about two inches. The jolt probably loosened a fill tube in oxygen tank 2, so two weeks before launch it would not empty, and technicians left its heaters on for some eight hours to drive the oxygen out. Thermostatic switches guarded those heaters, but a 1965 change had raised the pad's ground power from 28 to 65 volts, and those two switches alone were never requalified for it. Inside, temperatures on the heater tubes may have climbed to 540 degrees Celsius, cooking the insulation off the wires. Nobody noticed, because the tank's temperature gauge only read up to about 29 degrees, a little above room temperature, and simply sat at its top mark. A reading of normal can mean the fault is off the end of the scale.

archimedes-and-the-lever.context_blurb:
Archimedes of Syracuse, the great Greek mathematician of the third century BC, is remembered for a boast: give him somewhere to stand and a long enough lever, and he would move the whole Earth. He may never have said it. The line comes to us from Pappus of Alexandria, writing some five hundred years after Archimedes died, and it appears nowhere in his own surviving books.

Another tale comes from the biographer Plutarch. When King Hiero wanted proof that such ideas could do real work, Archimedes, by Plutarch's account, dragged a fully laden warship from the sea by himself with a compound pulley, a block and tackle in which every extra wheel trades force for a longer pull of rope. Another ancient writer tells it differently, so this too is story.

What Archimedes truly left is better than a boast: a proof. In his book On the Equilibrium of Planes he showed, step by step in the manner of Euclid's geometry, that two weights on a lever balance when each weight multiplied by its distance from the pivot gives the same number on both sides.

The price is always paid in distance. Imagine a girl on a seesaw who can press down with just one tenth of her heavier friend's weight. She can still raise her friend, but only if her own end travels ten times as far as her friend rises. Work in equals work out: levers, pulleys, ramps and screws multiply force only by spending distance, and none creates energy. Feel it yourself with a ruler balanced on a pencil and coins on each end.

Legend adds that Archimedes set Roman ships ablaze with mirrors when Rome besieged Syracuse in 212 BC, though the earliest historians of the siege never mention it. When MIT students in 2005 and then the MythBusters team in 2010 aimed many mirrors at a wooden mock-up held still, they got smoke and scorched timber but never a fire that kept burning.

Take the boast at its word anyway. To lift the Earth one centimetre with his own weight on the long end, Archimedes would have to push his end through roughly 10 to the power of 21 metres, farther than the Milky Way is wide. At walking pace that would take vastly longer than a human life, longer even than the age of the universe. The boast is poetry, but the law behind it is exactly right and still runs every crowbar and wheelbarrow.

archimedes-crown-and-the-balance-that-wo.context_blurb:
The famous story says a king of Syracuse suspected his goldsmith of mixing cheap silver into a golden wreath, and that Archimedes solved it in the bath and ran out shouting that he had found it. The tale reaches us only from the Roman writer Vitruvius, two centuries later, and the bath scene is probably legend. The principle behind it is real, and it governs everything that floats.

Start with a puzzle. A steel nail goes straight to the bottom, because steel is about eight times as dense as water, yet a steel cargo ship floats. Its hull wraps around so much air that the ship as a whole, steel plus air, averages out lighter than water. You can change the other side of the contest in a kitchen tonight. A raw egg sinks in tap water, but stir plenty of salt into the glass and the same egg rises. The salt adds weight to every cupful of water without adding much volume, so the water becomes denser than the egg.

Archimedes set out the rule in his book On Floating Bodies. Water pushes up on anything held in it with a force equal to the weight of the water that the object shoves out of the way. Why upward? Still water squeezes a submerged block from every side, but its pressure grows with depth, so the block's lower face is pressed harder than its upper face. The side pushes cancel; only the difference between bottom and top survives, and it equals exactly the weight of the water displaced.

In 1586 a 22-year-old Galileo wrote a short treatise, The Little Balance, about the usual version of the wreath story, where the wreath goes into a full bowl and the overflow is measured. He dismissed that method as crude and far from scientific precision, unworthy of Archimedes. The mathematician Chris Rorres later checked it. A kilogram of pure gold and a kilogram wreath of 70 percent gold and 30 percent silver, each lowered into a bowl 20 centimetres wide, raise the water by amounts less than half a millimetre apart, thinner than a credit card.

Galileo's better idea was a balance. Hang the gold on one arm and the wreath of equal weight on the other, and the beam hangs level in air. Lower both under water and the bulkier wreath, shoving aside more water, loses more of its weight, so the two now differ by about 13 grams, a gap any balance of Archimedes' day could detect. To read small differences, Galileo wound steel wire around the gold and silver marks on the arm and fine brass wire between them, then counted the turns by drawing a sharp stiletto slowly over the wires, hearing and feeling each one pass.

Buoyancy works in air too, because air is a fluid. A helium balloon rises because the air it shoves aside outweighs it. Put it in a sealed chamber, remove all the air from around it and let go, and it drops to the floor: with nothing to displace, there is no push.

The same rule became an instrument. Around AD 402 Synesius of Cyrene wrote to his old teacher in Alexandria, Hypatia, asking for a flute-shaped tube, sealed and weighted so it stood upright in water and notched along its length for testing the weight of waters. It is the oldest surviving description of a hydrometer, which sinks until it has displaced its own weight, riding high in dense water and deep in thin. A drinking straw plugged at one end with modelling clay makes one tonight.

Even a good rule has edges. Two physicists, Jeffrey Bierman and Eric Kincanon, tested one in 2003 by sealing a flat block to a tank's floor so no water could get beneath it. With nothing pushing from below, the water only pressed the block down, harder with every centimetre of depth above it. The principle holds for an object surrounded by fluid. The other edge is size. A needle dropped tip-first goes straight down, but laid flat with care on still water it floats. Surface tension, the water's skin, holds it up, and that force beats weight only for things a few millimetres across.

arrhenius-does-it-by-hand-and-the-forty-.context_blurb:
In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius worked thousands of sums by hand and produced the first estimate of greenhouse warming. He was trying to explain the ice ages, not to warn about the future. His idea was then buried for forty years by a careful but mistaken experiment, and dug up again by an amateur.

Arrhenius was used to being doubted. The doctoral thesis he defended at Uppsala in 1884 argued that dissolved salts split into electrically charged particles; his examiners thought that absurd and gave it fourth class, the lowest passing grade. In 1903 the same idea earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first won by a Swede.

Climate began as a side project. In November 1894 the geologist Arvid Högbom presented a ledger of carbon dioxide to the Swedish Chemical Society: volcanoes and hot springs adding the gas, rocks and the ocean taking it back. One human entry already rivalled the natural ones, the coal burning in the furnaces of industry. The question of whether changing the gas could change the ground's temperature came up afterwards, and Arrhenius went home to calculate.

He wanted to know what had buried Europe under ice sheets and then released it. Through most of 1895 he split the globe into bands ten degrees of latitude wide, worked each through four seasons, and tried amounts of the gas from two thirds of the real figure up to three times it. With no instrument to measure how strongly the gas absorbs heat, he borrowed numbers from the American astronomer Samuel Langley, who had measured the heat of the Moon arriving through different thicknesses of air.

His tables gave a headline: twice the carbon dioxide, about five to six degrees Celsius more warmth. The warming was not spread evenly: it piled up toward the poles, reaching 10 or 12 degrees in the far north and south. At the rate coal was then burned, he reckoned the doubling would take perhaps three thousand years. He was no prophet of doom. In his 1908 book Worlds in the Making he looked forward to the warming, hoping it would bring milder, steadier climates for the good of a growing mankind.

The setback came in 1900, when Knut Ångström, a Swedish physicist, tested the idea. His assistant, known to history only as Herr J. Koch, passed infrared rays through carbon dioxide in a tube 30 centimetres long, then took out a third of the gas; the absorption hardly changed. Physicists decided the gas already soaked up all it could. But such a tube holds a slice of air, not a sky: to match the gas standing over a patch of ground it would have needed to be about 250 centimetres long, eight times longer.

The man who revived the idea was no climate scientist. Guy Stewart Callendar was a steam technologist who, with his father, compiled the steam tables that turbine engineers used; climate was a hobby he worked out by hand at home. His 1938 talk to Britain's Royal Meteorological Society claimed some 0.3 degrees of warming of the world's land over half a century, caused by more carbon dioxide. The Met Office chief, Sir George Simpson, waved the match away as probably coincidence, for a real reason: he held that the air's temperature is set by air rising and sinking, not by radiation. On that narrow point Simpson was right, since Callendar had left out convection. In the Second World War he helped build FIDO, lines of gas burners along British runways that burned off the fog so bombers could land.

In 1956 Gilbert Plass redid the arithmetic with modern infrared data and got about 3.6 degrees for a doubling. He knew how infrared rays move through the atmosphere from his day job, designing infrared guidance for Lockheed's heat-seeking missiles.

The answer to Ångström came with that better physics. Koch's measurement was not wrong: low down, carbon dioxide really does absorb nearly all it can. But the Earth sheds its heat to space from the thin, cold air high up, and adding gas lifts that escape level higher, where it is colder and radiates less, so the planet must warm until the balance returns.

Arrhenius had already revised his own headline. In a 1906 paper he cut it to about 1.6 degrees, or roughly 2 once water vapour was counted. Scientists today still argue over a range of about 1.5 to 4.5 degrees.

ball-lightning-the-anomaly-in-the-unexpl.context_blurb:
For centuries, people caught in thunderstorms have reported a glowing ball that drifts along about a metre above the ground, lasts a few seconds and sometimes ends with a bang. Science has long accepted that ball lightning is real. What it is made of, and what makes it, nobody yet knows for sure.

One of the oldest detailed English accounts comes from Widecombe on Dartmoor. On 21 October 1638, during the Sunday service at St Pancras church, worshippers saw a huge ball of fire come in out of the storm. There it hung, broke into two and burst, tearing open the roof and killing four people. The congregation smelled brimstone and blamed the devil; the name ball lightning did not yet exist.

Reports from across centuries and continents agree remarkably well. The ball is usually 10 to 30 centimetres across, somewhere between a grapefruit and a soccer ball, and drifts sideways at walking pace. Witnesses often mention a smell of ozone or sulphur, and now and then a ball passes through a closed window.

It can kill. In St Petersburg on 6 August 1753, a physicist named Richmann, following up Benjamin Franklin's kite experiments, had an iron rod set up at home to measure the electricity of a storm when a glowing ball of lightning struck him on the forehead and killed him at once. He is generally counted as the first person killed while doing electrical research.

Ball lightning is often confused with St Elmo's fire, the bluish glow that sailors have long seen on masts during electrical storms and pilots see on wingtips. The giveaway is attachment: St Elmo's fire clings to a mast or a wingtip, while a ball floats free.

Nobody recorded one with instruments for nearly three centuries after Widecombe. Then in July 2012, on the Qinghai grasslands of China, Ping Yuan's team from Northwest Normal University in Lanzhou had cameras and spectrographs trained on ordinary lightning when, by pure luck, a ball appeared in their view about a kilometre away. It drifted a few metres, changed from purple to orange to white to red, and faded in under two seconds.

The spectrograph split the ball's light into its colours, and three lines stood out: silicon, iron and calcium, the elements of the soil beneath the strike. The glow came from the ground, not the air. That lends weight to the leading laboratory hypothesis, but it remains a hypothesis.

banting-best-and-a-summer-that-emptied-t.context_blurb:
Before 1922, a child with what we now call type 1 diabetes rarely lived a year. The best medicine had was Frederick Allen's starvation plan: 400 to 500 calories a day, almost all fat and protein. His wards smelled of acetone as patients burned their own bodies for fuel, and the diet bought months, not years. Then a team in Toronto found insulin.

Scientists had known since 1889 that the pancreas mattered. That year in Strasbourg, Joseph von Mering bet that no dog could live without its pancreas, and Oskar Minkowski removed one to settle it. The dog lived, but within a day its urine was five percent sugar. For thirty-two years nobody could get the controlling substance out of the gland intact.

Frederick Banting, a struggling young surgeon in London, Ontario, found a way in the middle of the night. After preparing a lecture on the pancreas in October 1920 he could not sleep, so in the small hours he got up and wrote a short note, two words misspelled, telling himself to tie off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, wait, and extract what survived. The waiting was the key. Tying the duct makes the part of the gland that produces digestive juice wither away, while the islets that make the hormone live on. That mattered because the juice, rich in trypsin, which digests protein, had been wrecking the protein hormone in every earlier extract.

In May 1921 the Toronto professor J.J.R. Macleod lent Banting a hot attic laboratory, about ten dogs and a student assistant. Edward Clark Noble and Charles Best, two new graduates, were to split the summer, and a coin toss sent Best first. By the end of his month Best had become skilled at the surgery, switching hands seemed unwise, and Noble never got his turn. The extracts spoiled and dogs died, and when the supply ran out the two men bought stray dogs off Toronto's streets for one to three dollars apiece. The tale that Banting sold his car to buy dogs cannot be confirmed.

That December they started injections in Marjorie, a dog whose pancreas had been removed, number 33 in the lab books, and the extract held her stable and alive for some seventy days. A missing organ could be made up for with a missing substance.

The extract was still dirty. The biochemist James Collip joined in December 1921 to purify it, and by late January 1922 he had the method: push the alcohol in the extract above ninety percent, and the other proteins can no longer stay dissolved and drop out, leaving the hormone behind. When Collip announced that he would share his method only with Macleod, Banting lost his temper, grabbed him by the overcoat and sat him down hard in a chair. Best pulled them apart, and an uneasy truce kept the team together.

The first human trial had already failed. Leonard Thompson, a boy of thirteen or fourteen weighing sixty-five pounds, received the crude extract on 11 January 1922: his blood sugar barely moved, and an abscess swelled where the needle went in. Twelve days later he got Collip's purified extract, and within a day his sugar was normal. He lived thirteen more years.

Elizabeth Hughes, whose father was the American Secretary of State, arrived in Toronto in the summer of 1922 weighing under fifty pounds. She lived another fifty-eight years on insulin, yet hid her diabetes from nearly everyone she knew. In October 1922, at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, eleven-year-old Elsie Needham became the first patient anywhere revived from a diabetic coma. The famous scene of the discoverers walking a ward of dying children and waking them one by one is legend; the true record is astonishing enough.

When the Nobel committee honoured Banting and Macleod in 1923, Banting was furious that Best was left out while Macleod had been holidaying in Scotland for part of that summer. He telegraphed Best that he was splitting his half of the money with him. Macleod then split his own half with Collip. The easy version makes Macleod a freeloader, but he supplied the lab, the dogs and the methods, recruited Collip and directed the work, and Toronto's centennial monument now carries all four names.

barry-marshall-drinks-the-beaker.context_blurb:
For most of the twentieth century, doctors were sure that stomach ulcers came from acid, stress and nerves. Two doctors in Perth, Australia, the pathologist Robin Warren and the young physician Barry Marshall, argued that a spiral bacterium was to blame, and Marshall finally proved it by swallowing the germ himself. Their Nobel Prize came twenty-one years later.

The old treatment followed a 1910 slogan, "no acid, no ulcer". From 1915, Bertram Sippy's regimen had patients sip milk mixed with cream every hour through the day, with alkaline powders in between, to soothe the acid. Later came antacids and, from 1976, acid-blocking pills taken more or less forever. Killing a germ was never part of the plan.

The boldest cure was surgery. Surgeons following Lester Dragstedt severed the vagus nerve, which signals the stomach to pour out acid, and by the 1960s American surgeons were doing more than 100,000 ulcer operations a year. A fifth to a third of patients were left with dumping syndrome: the stomach lost control of the pace of digestion, so food rushed through the gut and left them sweating and faint after meals.

In 1981 Warren, working in the basement pathology department of Royal Perth Hospital, had been finding curved bacteria in stomach biopsies. His list of those patients included a woman on Marshall's own ward, who had suffered severe pain for months without a diagnosis and whom his team in desperation had referred to a psychiatrist and put on antidepressants. When the tests found nothing, the patient's mind became the diagnosis.

Every expert said nothing could live in stomach acid. Helicobacter pylori manages it with chemistry. Hidden in the mucus layer, it produces urease, an enzyme that breaks down the urea already present in the stomach's fluid, and one product is ammonia, which cancels the acid in a small bubble around each bacterium. "The stomach is sterile" had been an assumption, not a measurement.

Growing the bug was the next wall. For months Marshall's culture plates came back empty, because lab routine threw them out after two days. Then, as Marshall tells it, one batch sat in the incubator through the Easter holiday of 1982, and when the staff came back it was covered in colonies of Warren's bacterium. The slow-growing organism had simply needed more time.

Marshall's study of a hundred patients then found the bacterium in every one with a duodenal ulcer. An Australian medical society rejected his abstract, a Perth meeting shrugged, and his own hospital declined to renew his contract.

To blame a germ for a disease, you must show it can sicken a healthy body, and Marshall's pigs carried the bacteria without ever falling ill. So in July 1984 he swallowed a beaker of the culture himself, about a billion organisms on an empty stomach. Within days he was vomiting in the mornings, sweating at night and breathing foul enough for his family to notice. On day ten a colleague's scope found the stomach lining raw and inflamed, but no ulcer. He had given himself gastritis, which largely cleared within two weeks.

When the 1985 paper came out in an Australian medical journal, its abstract called the man who drank the culture only "a volunteer" and never said which of the four authors he was. In the autobiography he wrote for the Nobel Foundation, Marshall later admitted that he had never taken the experiment to the hospital's ethics committee, the panel that must approve any test on a human being, and had not fully discussed it with his wife, Adrienne, either. Defenders say he risked only himself; critics answer that he could not know how bad it would be, and he admitted the infection's severity surprised him.

Marshall and Warren were right: the bacterium lies behind more than nine in ten duodenal ulcers, and getting rid of it heals them. Yet about half of all humans carry it, and only some 10 to 20 percent of carriers ever develop ulcer disease; most never feel a thing. What decides who falls ill is still argued over. Acid was not the cause, but it still matters. Today's treatment pairs two weeks of antibiotics and bismuth with a proton pump inhibitor, a drug that switches off the acid pumps in the stomach wall, and for a duodenal ulcer that drug continues for weeks afterward so the sore can heal in peace.

beaumonts-window-into-a-living-stomach.context_blurb:
In June 1822 a shotgun blast at close range tore open the side of Alexis St. Martin, a young French-Canadian voyageur, on Mackinac Island, at a fur-trading post. Nobody expected him to live, least of all the army surgeon who treated him, William Beaumont. Instead the wound gave medicine its first living window into a working human stomach, and raised hard questions about how that window was used.

As St. Martin healed, the torn stomach wall fused with the torn skin, leaving a permanent opening from his stomach to the outside, called a gastric fistula. Beaumont could now look and reach straight into a living stomach.

He used it to time digestion. He tied bits of raw cabbage, bread or beef to a silk thread, lowered them through the opening, and pulled them back out after set intervals to see how far the stomach had dissolved them. He also drew off gastric juice to test whether food would digest in a glass outside the body.

Day after day he watched the stomach change. Its lining sometimes reddened and sometimes went pale, and it worked fast one day and slowly the next. Checking his notes against St. Martin's moods, Beaumont became the first to show in a living person that anger and fear slow digestion down. During one fit of temper he even saw yellow bile flowing back into the stomach.

The science rested on one poor, illiterate man. St. Martin signed a written contract making him Beaumont's paid servant, bound to submit to experiments whenever asked. He ran home to Quebec in 1825, and Beaumont spent some twenty years trying to get him back. Beaumont's 1833 book founded the study of digestion in America, and the cost to St. Martin belongs to that record too.

St. Martin carried his open stomach for nearly six decades, died in Quebec in 1880, and outlived his doctor by 27 years. His family feared that anatomists would dig up the famous body, so they let it rot above ground before they buried it. A decayed stomach was worthless to any museum.

becquerels-drawer-radioactivity-found-by.context_blurb:
In Paris in February 1896, Henri Becquerel, from a family that had studied glowing minerals for three generations, set out to test an idea about uranium. A week of clouds ruined the plan and handed him radioactivity.

He wrapped a photographic plate in thick black paper and laid uranium crystals and a small metal cross on top, meaning to let sunlight charge the crystals first. The Sun stayed hidden, so he put everything away in a dark drawer, and on 1 March he developed the plate anyway. It was strongly exposed, with the silhouettes of the crystals and the cross standing out clearly.

His working idea had been that sunlight stored energy in the crystals, which then gave it back as rays. The drawer killed that idea: the uranium had sat in the dark all week and still exposed the plate, so it must give off rays all by itself, constantly, needing no light or heat at all. His mistaken hypothesis failed the test, and that failure was the discovery.

Radiation could also hurt. In April 1901 a little glass vial of radium rode in Becquerel's waistcoat pocket for a few hours. A fortnight later the skin beneath it broke into a raw sore shaped exactly like the tube, and it took months to heal. He published the burn, and his report helped launch radiotherapy, the use of radiation to attack tumours; in Vienna in 1902 doctors treated a throat cancer with radium.

before-jenner-montagu-onesimus-and-boyls.context_blurb:
Before Edward Jenner's cowpox vaccine, people fought smallpox with a far riskier method: variolation, also called engrafting or inoculation. Matter from a real smallpox sore went into a small cut, giving a healthy person a milder case and lasting protection. Long practised in parts of Africa and Asia, it reached Britain and America in the 1710s and 1720s, and in Boston it met the first medical statistics.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu knew the disease personally: it had scarred her face and killed her brother. In Constantinople in 1717 she wrote home about Turkish "engrafting parties", where women nicked the skin with a needle and worked in pus from someone else's smallpox sore. She had her own son treated there and carried the method home.

In Boston the Puritan minister Cotton Mather learned of it from Onesimus, a West African man whom Mather held in slavery. Onesimus showed him a small round scar and explained that the procedure had protected him from smallpox. Mather questioned other West Africans and read Turkish reports, and by the epidemic of 1721 he was the method's loudest champion.

Only one Boston doctor, Zabdiel Boylston, agreed to try it, and he did something more important: he counted. Of his 282 inoculated patients, 6 died; of the 5,759 Bostonians who caught smallpox naturally, 844 died. That careful comparison made his report the first clinical trial built on statistics, numbers set against authority. The method was not safe, because it used real smallpox: one or two in every hundred engrafted people died of it, against roughly three in ten who caught the disease in the ordinary way.

Numbers did not end the fight. One November night in 1721 someone flung a lit grenade into Mather's house, with a note cursing him. The fuse was knocked loose when the shell hit the floor, so the powder never went off.

Engrafting also carried a public danger. While their sores formed and healed, inoculated people had real, catching smallpox and could start an outbreak, so communities kept them away from healthy people until the sores had crusted over and dried, usually for a week or two. That rule was hard to enforce, and Jenner's cowpox, which spread no smallpox, would later escape the problem.

London ran its own test. On 9 August 1721, in the "Royal Experiment", six condemned prisoners at Newgate were promised pardons if they would be engrafted while physicians of the Royal College watched. The surgeon Charles Maitland cut incisions into both arms and the right leg of each prisoner, three sites to make the graft more likely to take. All six lived and went free.

bems-precognition-paper-lights-the-fuse.context_blurb:
In 2011 Daryl Bem, a respected Cornell psychologist who taught research methods, published nine experiments suggesting that college students could feel the future. In one, students guessed which of two curtains hid a picture slightly better than chance, before the computer had even chosen. Nobody found fraud. The shock was that the field's normal methods had produced the result.

The paper, "Feeling the Future", helped set off the replication crisis, the discovery that many published findings in psychology and beyond cannot be repeated. Where it appeared mattered. It ran in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the field's flagship; a fringe journal printing it would have been ignored, but the flagship's own gatekeepers had approved it, so mainstream psychology owned the result.

Then came the test that matters most: doing it again. Three researchers, Chris French, Richard Wiseman and Stuart Ritchie, ran Bem's ninth experiment again in 2012, at three universities and with his own software. All three runs came up empty, with no effect whatever.

Getting that news printed was harder. Three major journals turned the paper away without sending it to reviewers, each giving the same reason: it was only a replication, not a new finding. When the British Journal of Psychology did send it out, the authors suspected the second reviewer, and Bem later confirmed it: he had refereed the attempt to repeat his own work. The editor refused their request for a third referee. The paper finally appeared in the open-access journal PLoS ONE as "Failing the Future".

Statisticians went back to Bem's own numbers. Eric-Jan Wagenmakers, a Dutch statistician, led a team that reanalysed them with Bayesian statistics, a different way of weighing evidence, and found that the data actually favoured no psychic effect at all. The standard tests, they argued, could make weak evidence look strong, so the problem lay in the toolkit the whole field used.

Bem himself was candid. In a 2017 interview with Slate he said he had used data as a way to persuade, and that he had never really worried about whether his findings would replicate. Many readers heard that as nearly a confession of p-hacking, tuning an analysis until it crosses the bar for significance. His paper was never shown to be fraudulent; what failed was replication, the test that counts.

benedictuss-flask.context_blurb:
Every car windshield today owes something to a dropped flask. One day in 1903, in his Paris laboratory, the chemist Édouard Benedictus sent a glass flask tumbling from a high shelf to the floor, and went to sweep up the pieces.

There was nothing to sweep. The flask had cracked all over, yet it still held its shape, its shards locked in place like a spider's web. A film of cellulose nitrate, left to dry on the inside, had glued the broken glass together. Benedictus noted the oddity and put the flask aside.

For six years the accident waited for a use. In 1909 newspaper stories of drivers and passengers slashed by flying windshield glass in the first motor accidents brought the flask back to his mind. He patented a thin layer of transparent plastic between two panes of glass, and in 1911 he founded a company, the Société du Verre Triplex, to sell this safety glass, made above all to protect the car windshield.

Carmakers at first thought it cost too much. The First World War gave it its first big market instead, in the eyepieces of the gas masks the Allies issued, where a lens that cracks but stays whole is exactly what a soldier needs between his face and a cloud of chlorine.

Cars caught up only in the late 1920s. Henry Ford made laminated safety glass standard on the Model A, but only in the windshield, the pane a driver's face would hit first in a crash, while the other windows kept plain plate glass until 1931.

Look at a parked car tonight. Its windshield is still a Benedictus sandwich of glass, plastic and glass, but the plastic is now polyvinyl butyral, called PVB, which replaced cellulose nitrate in the 1930s because the old film yellowed in sunlight and could burn. In a crash it crazes into a web and stays in the frame. The side windows use a different fix, tempered glass that bursts into small pebbles.

big-bang-was-the-rivals-word.context_blurb:
By the middle of the twentieth century two serious theories competed to describe the universe. In one, everything began hot and dense and has been expanding ever since. In the other, the steady-state theory, the universe always looks much the same, because new matter quietly appears to fill the gaps as space expands. The first theory's famous name came from the second theory's champion.

On 28 March 1949, speaking on the BBC's Third Programme, the astronomer Fred Hoyle, a co-author of the steady-state theory, described his rivals' picture as "this big bang idea".

The story told everywhere is that Hoyle meant it as a sneer. Helge Kragh, a historian of science, checked the broadcast scripts and Hoyle's own statements and found that tale popular but poorly supported: Hoyle denied any mockery, and the record does not back it up. Hoyle explained that on radio, with no pictures to help him, he was always hunting for vivid images.

Steady state was real science because it made a risky prediction: if the universe never changes, very distant radio sources, seen as they were long ago, should look like nearby ones. Through the 1950s Martin Ryle's radio surveys at Cambridge tested it and found far too many faint, distant sources, so the young universe had been different from today's.

The 1965 discovery of the faint microwave hiss left over from the hot beginning ended steady state's run as a leading theory. Even so, cosmologists only took up "big bang" as the standard name in the 1970s, after the theory had already won; Gamow and his colleagues had long preferred other terms.

Hoyle never gave in, defending versions of steady state until his death. Yet historians add that he was magnificently right about another huge question. In 1957 he, Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge and William Fowler showed that the elements heavier than helium are cooked inside stars. Fowler alone received the 1983 Nobel Prize for that work, an omission widely seen as a snub.

black-holes-from-a-trench-on-the-russian.context_blurb:
Black holes began as mathematics written in a war zone and ended up in a photograph. Along the way the idea was doubted, attacked from the podium and finally proved, by an artillery officer, a teenager at sea, a mathematician and a worldwide network of radio dishes.

In November 1915 Albert Einstein completed general relativity and expected exact solutions to his equations to take years. Within weeks a letter arrived from Karl Schwarzschild, an astronomer then serving as a German artillery officer on the Russian front, who had solved them by hand for a spherical mass, a solution that describes what we now call a black hole. His letter thanked the war for letting him take this walk in Einstein's land of ideas.

Schwarzschild, who had volunteered past the age of forty, never saw the war end. At the front he caught pemphigus, a rare skin disease in which the immune system attacks the body, and he died of it in May 1916, aged 42.

For decades the dark centre of his solution was treated as a mathematical oddity rather than a real place, and it had no catchy name. Beginning in 1967, John Wheeler, an American physicist, made one famous in his lectures: black hole. He did not coin it; the phrase had already appeared at meetings in 1963 and 1964.

In 1930, sailing to England for a scholarship at Cambridge, nineteen-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated the fate of a dead star. Any burnt-out star heavier than roughly 1.44 Suns, he found, cannot hold itself up and must keep collapsing, into a neutron star or a black hole. When he presented the result to the Royal Astronomical Society in January 1935, Arthur Eddington, hero of the 1919 eclipse and the most powerful astrophysicist in Britain, rose next and attacked it in public as physically meaningless. Eddington believed some unknown physics would halt the collapse. Chandrasekhar was right, and his Nobel Prize came forty-eight years later.

Doubters still argued that a real star, lumpy and spinning, would escape collapsing to a point. In 1965 the British mathematician Roger Penrose proved otherwise: once collapse traps even outgoing light inside a closed surface, a singularity at the centre cannot be avoided.

Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics with two astronomers, Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez. For decades their teams, at telescopes in Chile and in Hawaii, followed individual stars racing around something unseen at our galaxy's centre, about four million times the Sun's mass.

Then came the picture. The Event Horizon Telescope released an image of the black hole in the galaxy M87 in April 2019, and one of our own galaxy's in May 2022. Radio dishes on four continents recorded raw signals onto hard drives, which were flown to central labs and combined. A black hole gives off no light, so what the image shows is its shadow, the dark patch it casts on the glowing hot gas around it, about 2.6 times wider than the event horizon.

boltzmann-the-atom-and-the-gravestone.context_blurb:
Ludwig Boltzmann, a physicist in Vienna in the late 1800s, argued that heat is nothing but the motion of countless invisible particles. Many leading scientists refused to believe in atoms they could not see, and he spent much of his career defending them. His most famous formula is carved on his gravestone.

A smashed egg shows his idea. No law of nature stops the pieces from jumping back together. It never happens because the scrambled arrangements of all those particles vastly outnumber the tidy ones, so tidiness never comes back by chance.

Critics attacked with mathematics. Ernst Zermelo used a new theorem by Henri Poincaré: any closed, bounded system must eventually wander back close to where it started, so entropy cannot climb forever. Boltzmann did not dispute the theorem. He reshaped the second law of thermodynamics instead: a spontaneous fall in entropy is not forbidden at all, merely so improbable that no one would ever see it.

Proof of atoms came later. Einstein predicted in 1905 how tiny grains in water should jitter as invisible molecules knock them about, and in 1908 and 1909 Jean Perrin, a physicist in France, tracked such grains under a microscope. His numbers matched, and they finally settled whether atoms are real objects. Even Wilhelm Ostwald, a leading doubter, gave in.

Boltzmann did not live to see it; he died by suicide at Duino, near Trieste, in September 1906. The tale usually told is that rejection broke him, but it leaves out something documented: he had suffered severe depression for years and had attempted suicide before, with mood swings like what would now be called bipolar disorder. Historians agree the true cause cannot be settled.

borlaugs-dwarf-wheat-and-the-famine-that.context_blurb:
In the 1960s respected scientists warned that hundreds of millions of people would soon starve, whatever farmers did. It did not happen, largely because of Norman Borlaug, an Iowa-born plant scientist who spent nearly two decades breeding wheat in Mexico. His trick is simple to picture: heavily fertilised wheat grows heads so heavy that the stalks fall over, so he made the plants shorter and sturdier.

The short wheat was not his invention. Its dwarfing genes came from Norin 10, a Japanese variety released by Gonjiro Inazuka in 1935. After the Second World War the American Cecil Salmon collected it in occupied Japan, Orville Vogel at Washington State bred it further, and in 1953 seed reached Borlaug. Those genes now sit in more than seventy percent of the world's commercial wheat.

When word came in October 1970 that the Nobel Peace Prize was his, his wife Margaret had to drive out to the fields near Toluca to find him. The news had come from a reporter at the Oslo paper Aftenposten, not through official channels, so Borlaug took it for a hoax and went on working.

He is often said to have saved a billion lives. That figure is a rough estimate rather than a count, and it entered print through Gregg Easterbrook's 1997 essay in The Atlantic, "Forgotten Benefactor of Humanity". A defensible estimate is still an estimate, even for a hero.

Borlaug himself refused to declare victory. In his Nobel lecture he warned that human population growth must also be curbed, and he stated flatly that agricultural production has no miracles: the pressure would return unless yields kept rising.

boyle-hooke-and-the-spring-of-the-air.context_blurb:
Block the tip of a syringe and press: the air inside fights back. Robert Boyle, an Anglo-Irish experimenter working with the young Robert Hooke in the 1660s, turned that push into one of the first laws of physics, though the law's name tells only part of the story.

Boyle called this resistance the air's spring, using the word as we still do for a metal coil: an elastic push-back. His 1660 book on air-pump experiments carried the phrase in its title.

Hooke's apparatus was a glass tube bent into a J, closed at the short end, where a pocket of air was trapped. Pouring mercury into the long arm squeezed that air, and mercury, a heavy liquid that does not cling to clean glass, presses hard even in a short column. Double the squeeze and the air shrank to half its volume.

Boyle never claimed the rule as his own idea. In print in 1662 he credited the hypothesis to two Lancashire experimenters, Richard Towneley and Henry Power, calling it Mr Towneley's hypothesis, and noted that Hooke had already confirmed it. In France the rule carries yet another name, Mariotte's law, after Edme Mariotte, who found it on his own in the 1670s and spelled out a requirement Boyle had skipped: the temperature has to stay fixed. Warm the gas and it expands even under the same squeeze.

Not everyone accepted Boyle's empty space. In 1661 the philosopher Thomas Hobbes, author of Leviathan, attacked the air pump in a book, insisting that nature allows no truly empty space, so the pumped glass had to be leaking. The Jesuit Franciscus Linus proposed that an invisible stretched thread, which he called the funiculus, Latin for "little rope", still filled the pumped-out glass. Boyle answered both with more experiments rather than more argument.

Why does air push back? For seventy years nobody could say. In his 1738 book Hydrodynamica, the Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli pictured a gas as countless tiny particles darting through emptiness, so that what we feel as pressure is their endless pelting of the container; squeeze the gas into half the room and each wall is struck twice as often.

Boyle had also shown that animals need air by pumping it away from mice, birds and other creatures sealed in his glass. A century later, travelling lecturers performed that demonstration as paid evening entertainment, and in 1768 the English painter Joseph Wright of Derby painted the scene by candlelight: a white cockatoo under the glass, a frightened child, and the lecturer gazing straight out at the viewer.
