brearleys-rustless-steel.context_blurb:
Stainless steel is in every kitchen, and it began with a hunt for something else. In 1912 the British Army wanted rifle barrels that would not wear away when fired, and the Sheffield metallurgist Harry Brearley was hired to find a tougher alloy.

The tougher barrel eluded him. Instead, in 1913, working with chromium-rich alloys, he found a steel that rust could not touch. He called it rustless steel; the world soon called it stainless.

The popular version has him spotting one bright sample in a rusting scrap pile. His own account is plainer. Before inspecting any new alloy under the microscope, he polished it and etched it with nitric acid to bring out its crystal structure, and on this alloy the acid simply would not bite.

The secret is a skin. When the alloy meets the air, its chromium reacts to form a film of chromium oxide only a few nanometres thick, which seals the metal from further attack. It needs roughly 10.5 to 12 percent chromium in the mix. Chrome plating peels away and leaves bare metal to rust, but this film heals itself: when it is scratched, chromium atoms from deep inside the alloy move to the wound and lay down a fresh film within minutes.

Brearley was not alone. Philipp Monnartz, a German, had proved in 1911 that iron with chromium above about 12 percent turns passive and shrugs off acid. And in October 1912 the German firm Krupp patented a chromium-nickel version, branded Nirosta, developed by its metallurgists Benno Strauss and Eduard Maurer. Several teams reached these alloys at nearly the same moment. What Brearley did that the others had not was recognise what he held and turn it into a product.

bretz-and-the-flood-nobody-would-believe.context_blurb:
Eastern Washington holds a strange landscape: bare rock canyons with no rivers in them, giant potholes, and Dry Falls, a dry waterfall cliff some three and a half miles across, higher than Niagara. In the 1920s the Chicago geologist J Harlen Bretz offered an explanation that most of his profession refused to accept for decades.

In 1923 Bretz claimed that one catastrophic flood had carved the whole region, which he named the Channeled Scablands.

His critics had a principled reason to resist. Geology had been rebuilt by Charles Lyell around uniformitarianism, the rule that the past is explained by the slow processes we can watch today, working at their present pace, and Lyell built it to shut out appeals to a biblical Flood that carved the land in a single event. To many geologists, Bretz's giant flood sounded like a step backwards.

Bretz also had a real gap: he could not say where such an enormous body of water had come from. On 12 January 1927 the Geological Society of Washington invited him to present his idea at the Cosmos Club, and after his talk six senior geologists, several from the US Geological Survey, rose one after another with rebuttals they had prepared in advance. Bretz later called it an ambush by invitation.

The answer came from Joseph Thomas Pardee of the US Geological Survey, working in Montana on the floor of a vanished lake, Glacial Lake Missoula. In 1940 he described ridges 5 to 10 metres tall shaped exactly like the little ripples on a stream bed: giant current ripples that only a sudden, colossal torrent draining the lake could have made. Pardee had found Bretz's missing water.

Later work showed the flood came not once but dozens of times; a single railway cutting near Missoula preserves 29 of them. A lobe of the great Cordilleran Ice Sheet kept advancing across the Clark Fork valley and damming it, the lake refilled behind the ice, and each time the dam floated loose and burst. At its peak the water poured out at about ten times the combined flow of all the world's rivers.

In 1979, aged 96, Bretz received the Geological Society of America's highest honour, the Penrose Medal. Afterwards, the story goes, he told his son that all his enemies were dead, so he had nobody left to gloat over. The lesson is not that the experts were fools; geology had to make room for rare, enormous events beside slow ones.

brownian-motion-how-pollen-made-atoms-re.context_blurb:
Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist who had just become the British Museum's first Keeper of Botany, was studying how plants are fertilised in 1827. Tiny specks in a drop of water under his microscope would not keep still, and the puzzle he found took eighty years to solve and ended by proving that atoms are real.

Hour after hour the specks jittered in endless zigzags and never settled. Because they had come from pollen, Brown's first guess was that he was watching life itself, some vital force at work inside living things. Then he attacked his own favourite idea.

He powdered whatever he could lay hands on, from window glass and lava to meteorites and metals, and tested each. One sample was a scraping from a fragment of the Sphinx. Every sample jiggled, so life had nothing to do with it. The usual retelling gets one detail wrong: a whole pollen grain is far too big to dance, and the dancers were far smaller particles, about 2 micrometres across, released from inside the grains. In 1828 Brown published his results and ended by admitting that he could not account for the motion.

Others had glimpsed it earlier. In 1785 the Dutch physician Jan Ingenhousz had noticed the same jiggling in specks of coal dust on the surface of alcohol, then moved on. Some historians later doubted that Brown's simple one-lens microscope could have shown the effect at all. Brian J Ford, a microscopist, settled it in 1992: he borrowed Brown's own microscope from the Linnean Society, repeated the experiment and filmed the specks jiggling through the original glass.

The cause was argued over for decades. Ludwig Boltzmann's kinetic theory explained heat as the motion of molecules, but followers of Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald held that physics should speak only of what can be perceived. Boltzmann had a long quarrel with the chief editor of the leading German physics journal, who insisted that atoms be described as handy fictions for calculation, never as real things.

In 1905 Albert Einstein turned the jiggle into a test. Do not measure a speck's speed, he said, because its path doubles back so often that any speed depends on how often you look. Track instead the distance a speck ends up from where it began, checked at one-minute intervals: that distance should increase with the square root of the time that has passed, so four times as long gives only twice as far.

In 1908 Jean Perrin, in Paris, took up the test. He rubbed a yellow resin, gamboge, under water and sorted the grains by size with months of centrifuging. Then two men took turns at the microscope, one calling time while the other marked each granule's position as a dot every 30 seconds. In his 1913 book Les Atomes, written for ordinary readers, Perrin gathered thirteen unrelated ways of counting molecules, from Brownian motion to the blue of the sky, and showed that all of them gave the same number.

The verdict changed minds. Wilhelm Ostwald had argued for two decades that only energy was real and chemistry needed no atoms. In his chemistry textbook's 1908 edition, its fourth, he wrote that the particle nature of matter had now been proved, crediting Perrin's work.

Boltzmann, who died in 1906, never saw it. Yet his formula, carved on his headstone in Vienna, counts the hidden arrangements that could produce what we see, and it is meaningless unless atoms exist. In 1900 Max Planck borrowed it to derive the law of how hot objects glow, and so opened the door to quantum theory.

The mathematics of the random walk reached further still. On 29 March 1900, five years before Einstein, a Paris doctoral student, Louis Bachelier, defended a thesis that used the same random process to model how prices drift up and down on the Paris stock exchange.

buys-ballots-trumpeters-on-the-open-rail.context_blurb:
In 1842 the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler argued that the pitch of a sound, or the colour of light, depends on whether its source is moving toward you or away. A Dutch scientist, Christophorus Buys Ballot, thought the idea was wrong and built a public experiment on the new railway to kill it.

His plan was to prove that Doppler was wrong and that no shift existed at all. He would seat horn players in an open wagon, have them hold one steady note as the train ran past, and station musicians with trained ears beside the line. The first attempt, in February 1845, collapsed when hail and snow made it impossible for the players to play.

He ran it again on 3 June 1845, on the Utrecht-Maarssen line, with the wagon doing about forty miles an hour. The listeners heard the note arrive about half a tone higher as the wagon came toward them and drop lower as it moved away. Buys Ballot had set out to refute Doppler and instead gave the effect its best early confirmation for sound.

Why does the note rise? The horn sends out crests at a steady rate, but the wagon is chasing its own sound, so each crest starts out a little nearer the listener than the one before. The crests arrive bunched together, which the ear hears as a higher pitch; behind the wagon they spread out and the pitch falls.

You can test this at the roadside. As an ambulance comes straight at you, its siren sounds steadily high; as it passes, the pitch drops abruptly; then it stays steadily low as it drives away. You hear a plateau, a step and a second plateau, not a slow slide, and the closer it passes, the sharper the step.

The effect now works everywhere. Shigeo Satomura of Osaka University aimed ultrasound at a patient's chest in December 1955 and found the echo shifted by something moving inside, and in 1962 Kanemasa Kato showed that the shifted echo came from red blood cells streaming through the heart. Today colour Doppler scans paint blood flowing toward the probe red and away from it blue. Astronomers read the same kind of shift in starlight: in 1995 the wobble of the star 51 Pegasi revealed a planet about as massive as Jupiter that circles its star in about four days, where Jupiter needs twelve years.

Doppler himself had pushed the idea too far. His 1842 paper on double stars claimed that their colours came from their motion, and that a white star rushing toward us faster and faster would turn green, then blue, then violet, until it vanished from sight. That part was wrong: a star's colour is set mainly by its surface temperature, and the stars' actual speeds are far too small to change a colour visibly.

A police radar gun uses the same physics with radio waves. Its formula divides the measured shift by two because the wave is shifted twice: once when the moving car meets it, and again when the car sends the echo back.

The optical idea was rescued in 1848 by the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau. Instead of a star's overall colour, he said, watch the narrow dark lines in its spectrum, which sit at fixed, known places; motion shifts those sharp lines even when no eye could see the colour change. Doppler never saw it work, dying in Venice in 1853.

In 1868 William Huggins used one of those lines, in the light of Sirius, to make the first measurement of any star's speed: about 40 kilometres a second, moving away. Sirius is actually approaching at about 5.5. His likeliest mistake was that he had not subtracted the Earth's own motion around the Sun, some 30 kilometres a second. Wrong in size and direction, the measurement still convinced scientists that the effect worked for light.

cajal-golgi-and-the-gap-between-neurons.context_blurb:
Does one nerve cell pass its message to the next through a continuous web, or across a gap? Camillo Golgi of Italy and Santiago Ramón y Cajal of Spain shared the 1906 Nobel Prize and gave opposite answers, and settling it took a stain, a chemical, two frog hearts and finally the electron microscope.

Golgi was chief physician at a home for incurable patients outside Milan, which had no laboratory, so he set up his bench in the kitchen of his own apartment there. In 1873 he produced his "black reaction", a silver stain that turns a few nerve cells jet black, every branch drawn out to its tip. Looking at those cells, Golgi concluded that they were all fused into one continuous net, and he defended that view all his life.

Oddly, the stain takes in only a few cells in every hundred, and nobody knows why. That defect is its strength: to follow a cell's branches you need a thick slice, and if every cell in it turned black you would see only a solid smear.

Doubts about the net came early. Four anatomists working independently in the decade after 1877 decided that nerve branches usually do not join, and one was Fridtjof Nansen, later famous for letting his ship Fram drift across the Arctic ice. As a museum curator in Bergen he learned Golgi's stain at Pavia in 1886 and applied it to sea creatures.

Cajal made the doubt impossible to ignore. Luis Simarro, a Madrid physician, had shown him silver-stained slides around 1887, and Cajal improved Golgi's recipe by putting the tissue through the silver bath twice. He also changed the specimen. Adult tissue was a jungle of fatty, tangled branches, so he stained embryos of birds and very young animals, whose simple nerve cells could be followed to their ends; why not study the young wood in the nursery, he asked. His papers, in Spanish, went unread in Germany, so in 1889 he carried his own microscopes to the anatomists' meeting in Berlin, each one with a slide ready under the lens, and made the Germans look for themselves.

The junction itself got a name in 1897, when Charles Sherrington wanted a word for the meeting point between two nerve cells. A classical scholar, Verrall, offered "synapse", from Greek words meaning to fasten together: the image is a clasp joining two things.

In Stockholm in 1906 the two rivals met for the first time. In his lecture on 11 December, with Cajal in the hall, Golgi attacked Cajal's neuron doctrine as a theory already going out of favour. Cajal replied the next day: a continuous net would indeed be convenient and economical, he granted, but nature seems not to care about our wish for convenience.

The chemistry came from Otto Loewi in 1921. He kept two frog hearts alive, each in its own bath of salt solution, stimulated the vagus nerve of the first until it slowed, then poured that heart's bath over the second heart, which had no nerve at all; it slowed too, so a dissolved chemical had carried the message. The chemical was acetylcholine. Loewi's tale that the idea came in a dream, scribbled at night and unreadable by morning, is doubted, because he told it himself decades later and liked to make a story dramatic. Other laboratories often failed to repeat the result. Loewi had been lucky: he worked in an unheated room in winter, and the cold slowed the enzyme that destroys the chemical, so enough of it survived the transfer.

Light microscopes cannot see below about 200 nanometres, so only a new instrument could end the argument. Sanford Palay and George Palade, using the electron microscope in 1954, measured a gap of about 20 nanometres between two membranes that run side by side but never merge, and on the sending side they saw a crowd of tiny round sacs, holding the chemical messenger, pressed against the membrane. Golgi was not wholly wrong, though. Edwin Furshpan and David Potter, probing a giant crayfish synapse in 1959, found almost no delay, because channels there join the insides of the two cells directly: an electrical synapse. Such junctions are the exception, not the rule.

carnots-perfect-engine-and-the-ceiling-n.context_blurb:
In 1824 Sadi Carnot, a young French army engineer, asked why British steam engines were beating French ones, and answered with a law that still caps every engine on Earth. He reasoned it out from a wrong theory of heat, published it at his own expense, and died before anyone noticed.

Carnot opened his book with a warning: without her steam engines England would lose her coal, her iron and all her wealth, a blow worse even than the destruction of her navy, which she considered her strongest defence. He was trying to frighten France, whose engines ran at about 3 percent efficiency. He set himself two questions nobody had settled: whether some other fluid, such as alcohol, might beat steam, and whether there is any upper limit to the power that fire can give. In 1819 the elite corps of state engineers had refused him though he passed its exam, most likely because his father, Lazare Carnot, a minister under Napoleon, was living in exile.

To picture something no one had words for, Carnot likened an engine to a waterfall turning a mill wheel. A waterfall's power depends on how much water falls and how far; in an engine, the height of the fall is the difference in temperature between the furnace and the cold side. Without cold, heat is useless. The fluid inside does not matter, he argued, and even something without any vapour could be a heat engine: a metal bar, growing longer as it is heated and shorter as it cools, could move whatever is fastened to its ends.

His proof was a thought experiment. Suppose some super-engine beat a perfectly reversible one between the same furnace and cold body. Spend part of its work driving the reversible engine backwards to restore the starting conditions, and you would have endless power from nothing, which Carnot ruled inadmissible. So every reversible engine between the same two temperatures is equally efficient, whatever its fuel or gears. The catch is that a perfectly reversible engine would have to work infinitely slowly and would therefore produce no power whatever.

The ceiling is simple to compute: subtract the cold temperature over the hot one from one. Both temperatures must be counted from absolute zero, in kelvin, not from the freezing point of water. Boiling water at 373 kelvin exhausting into a 298-kelvin room gives a ceiling of about 20 percent, not the 75 a careless sum suggests.

Today's most efficient heat engines, combined-cycle gas power stations, convert more than 60 percent of their fuel's heat to electricity. Their second stage is a plain steam plant: the hot exhaust of the gas turbine boils water to drive a second turbine. Engineers still climb toward Carnot's line in only the two ways he allowed, making the hot side hotter or the cold side colder.

Run Carnot's engine backwards and it becomes a refrigerator, pumping heat from cold to hot, with the same two temperatures setting its limit. Keep a fridge's inside at 271 kelvin while the room stands at 312, and each joule of work can at best move about seven joules of heat out of it: 271 divided by 41.

The first edition ran to 600 copies, paid for by Carnot himself. A friendly review praised it without explaining the reasoning, and by 1835 the edition was still unsold. The argument survived because the engineer Émile Clapeyron recast it in an 1834 memoir, drawing the cycle as a pressure-volume diagram for the first time. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, and Rudolf Clausius, who built thermodynamics' second law out of Carnot's ideas, never saw his book and knew it only through Clapeyron.

Carnot built all this on caloric, the theory that heat is a weightless fluid that flows from hot to cold and is never used up. The theory is false, yet believing it in 1824 was reasonable: engines then wasted so much that about 97 percent of the heat going in came out the far end, and the missing sliver hid inside the errors of the day's instruments. Cholera killed Carnot in 1832 at 36, and most of his papers were burned as a precaution, but his brother Hippolyte saved a notebook. In it Carnot called heat a form of motion and priced the trade: 2.70 units of heat spent for each unit of work, about two decades before James Joule measured it.

carrie-buck-and-the-rigged-test-case.context_blurb:
In 1927 the United States Supreme Court ruled that the state of Virginia could sterilize Carrie Buck, a young woman in its care, against her will. Behind the ruling stood the eugenics movement, which held that the "unfit" should be stopped from having children, and almost everything the public was told about Carrie's case was false.

The vote, on 2 May 1927, was eight to one. Writing for the majority, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. ended with the line that has followed the case ever since: three generations of imbeciles, he declared, were enough. The lone dissenter, Justice Pierce Butler, the Court's only Catholic, wrote nothing at all to explain his vote; the record is blank.

Carrie had been an ordinary pupil living with foster parents, the Dobbs family. What sent her at 17 to the state's colony for the "feeble-minded" was a pregnancy, and she said the nephew of her foster parents had raped her. Locking her away kept the scandal out of the household.

The case was manufactured. The Colony's superintendent, Albert Priddy, had been sterilizing women for years, but with Carrie he did something new: he pushed her case through the courts on purpose, to test Virginia's new 1924 sterilization law before the highest court. Priddy died in 1925, and his successor, John Bell, gave the case its name.

Carrie's defence was a sham. Paul Lombardo, a historian at the University of Virginia, later discovered that her court-appointed lawyer, Irving Whitehead, had sat on the Colony's own board and supported sterilization. Whitehead called no witnesses for her and conceded key facts.

The "third generation" was Carrie's baby daughter, Vivian. Arthur Estabrook of the Eugenics Record Office examined her once, at about seven months old, by holding a shiny coin in front of her eyes; he judged her response below average and told the court she was feebleminded. Vivian's later school records in Charlottesville tell a different story.

Holmes's legal engine was an analogy. In Jacobson v. Massachusetts in 1905 the Court had upheld compulsory vaccination, and Holmes argued that the principle behind forced vaccination was broad enough to cover cutting a woman's Fallopian tubes. A precedent about smallpox shots was stretched into surgery.

The ruling has never been overturned. Skinner v. Oklahoma, decided in 1942, struck down a law imposing vasectomy on three-time felons, but on the narrow ground of equal protection: Oklahoma sterilized repeat thieves while sparing embezzlers, an inconsistency Justice Douglas called irrational. That let the Court avoid ruling on eugenic sterilization itself.

Real science was pointing elsewhere all along. In the same decade Charles Stiles was tracking hookworm, a soil-borne parasite that drained the energy of poor Southerners, and Joseph Goldberger's careful diet experiments on prisoners proved that pellagra came from poor nutrition, not bad heredity. Many symptoms branded "feeblemindedness" had causes that doctors could find and fix.

casgevy-the-first-crispr-cure.context_blurb:
Sickle-cell disease comes from one wrong letter in one gene. In late 2023 it became the first illness treated by an approved CRISPR gene-editing therapy, Casgevy, and the road there runs from a 1949 laboratory to a mother in Mississippi.

Victoria Gray, who grew up in rural Mississippi and is a mother of four, spent her life in and out of hospital with attacks of pain that could last for weeks. She had sickle-cell disease, inherited through her family. In 2019 she became the first American patient treated in the trial that led to Casgevy, and since her infusion she has reported no crises and no hospital stays.

The trouble lies in hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen inside red blood cells. When oxygen runs low in the tissues, during hard exercise, at altitude or in illness, the faulty hemoglobin stacks into stiff fibres that bend the round cells into crescents, which jam in tiny vessels and starve the tissue of blood. In 1949 Linus Pauling's team ran sickle and normal hemoglobin through an electric field and watched them drift to different places, the first time a human disease had been tied to one faulty protein; Pauling called it a molecular disease. In the mid-1950s Vernon Ingram found the exact change: at position 6 of the hemoglobin beta chain, valine has replaced glutamic acid.

Babies make a different, fetal form of hemoglobin that does not sickle, and the body switches it off after birth. For decades doctors have used a drug, hydroxyurea, that turns some fetal hemoglobin back on and so dilutes the sickling kind.

Casgevy uses the same idea through CRISPR. It is often described as fixing the broken gene, but it does not touch the faulty hemoglobin gene at all. Instead it cuts a switch on a different gene, BCL11A, which normally shuts fetal hemoglobin off; with that gene silenced in the red-cell line, the fetal form comes back on and does the work. Doctors edit the patient's own blood stem cells outside the body and return them after harsh chemotherapy, which can cause infertility.

Britain's drug regulator, the MHRA, approved Casgevy first, in November 2023. The American Food and Drug Administration followed on 8 December 2023, clearing two sickle-cell gene therapies in a single day: Casgevy and Lyfgenia, which delivers a gene with a modified virus instead of CRISPR. In the pivotal trial, 29 of 31 evaluable patients went at least a year without a severe pain crisis, and the other two still had far fewer. The cure is real, and so is the cost: about $2.2 million for one treatment in the United States.

catalysts-changed-by-nothing-changing-ev.context_blurb:
A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, so when the reaction is done it is still there, ready to work again. You can watch one at a kitchen table with raw liver and a bottle of drugstore hydrogen peroxide, and the same idea runs car exhausts, fertiliser factories and every cell in your body.

Drop raw liver into peroxide and foam pours over the rim. Liver is packed with catalase, an enzyme that splits hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, and the bubbles are that oxygen gas escaping. Boil a second piece of liver first and it barely stirs the beaker. Nothing was washed away: the heat unfolded the catalase and warped it out of the shape it needs to work, and for an enzyme, shape is everything.

Catalase is astonishingly fast. Each molecule has four working sites and gets through about 40 million peroxide molecules every second. It is so quick that its chemistry is not what holds it back: a 2025 study of single catalase molecules confirmed that its top speed is set by how fast peroxide molecules can drift close enough to be grabbed.

Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner, a chemist at Jena, discovered in 1823 that hydrogen blown onto spongy platinum makes the metal glow and sets the gas alight, with no flame anywhere. He turned the trick into a lighter that made flame on demand, and some 20,000 were in use by 1828. In 1835 the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius gathered such puzzles, from acid turning starch to sugar to blood foaming peroxide, under one name, catalysis, and set a sharp test: the agent must speed the reaction yet come out unchanged in quantity and quality. The British chemist Elizabeth Fulhame had described the same give-it-back logic in 1794.

Catalysts feed the world. Fritz Haber first made ammonia from air in 1909, but his catalysts, osmium and uranium, were expensive. Alwin Mittasch of the German firm BASF went looking for something cheaper, running batteries of small reactors in parallel to test thousands of recipes. The winner was fused iron ore, the mineral magnetite, spiked with alumina and potash, and it is still used almost unchanged.

How does a catalyst work? Bottled hydrogen peroxide decomposes so slowly that you would wait days for a bubble, but add a pinch of manganese dioxide powder and it foams within seconds; afterwards you can filter the powder out and reuse it. The powder opens an easier route that lowers the energy barrier, the hill the molecules must get over, like a lower pass through the same mountains. It adds no energy and never changes where the reaction finally ends up; it only gets there sooner.

Much of the action happens on surfaces. Between 1916 and 1918 Irving Langmuir of General Electric showed that a gas landing on clean metal settles as a single layer just one molecule deep. If only that outer layer reacts, surface area is everything, which is why catalysts are built as sponges, powders and honeycombs.

Catalysts can also be poisoned. From 1975, American cars carried catalytic converters whose platinum and palladium burned the carbon monoxide and leftover fuel in the exhaust. A single tank of leaded petrol could kill one for good, because the lead coats the precious metals and alloys with them.

A catalyst can do harm, too. The chemists Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland traced CFC refrigerant gases up into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks a chlorine atom loose. The chlorine takes one oxygen atom from an ozone molecule, and then a loose oxygen atom pulls that oxygen away again, freeing the chlorine to repeat the cycle. One atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.

The champion catalysts are enzymes. Left in water at room temperature, orotic acid takes 78 million years for half of it to lose its carbon dioxide. Anna Radzicka and Richard Wolfenden timed the enzyme that does this step in your cells, in 1995: about 18 milliseconds. That is a speed-up of roughly a hundred million billion times, with no energy added.

cavendish-weighs-the-world.context_blurb:
In 1797 and 1798, in a sealed shed in his garden at Clapham Common in London, the famously shy scientist Henry Cavendish carried out what became known as weighing the world. He measured the faint gravitational tug between lead balls, and from it worked out how dense the whole Earth is.

The instrument was not his own. John Michell, a country rector and amateur geologist in Yorkshire, had designed the twisting torsion balance, but he died with it still unused, and the apparatus passed to Cavendish, who rebuilt it and kept close to Michell's plan.

The tug was so tiny that the warmth of his own body would have stirred the air in the shed and swamped it. So Cavendish never went in while it ran: he watched the balance through a telescope set up outside the shed.

His 1798 paper, "Experiments to determine the Density of the Earth", gave only one number about the planet: its mean density, as a multiple of the density of water. From that the Earth's mass follows, and from mass and size, everything else.

He printed 5.48: the Earth, he found, is about five and a half times as dense as water. That is less than one percent from today's value of 5.514. Francis Baily, an astronomer, went back over Cavendish's 29 results in 1821 and found a minor arithmetic mistake in the average Cavendish had computed; Baily's corrected figure was 5.448.

Textbooks often credit Cavendish with measuring big G, the constant in Newton's law of gravity, but he never used that letter or that term; his quarry was density. Alfred Cornu, working with Baille, first extracted a value of G from Cavendish's data in 1873.

Michell had another idea far ahead of its time. In November 1783 he wrote to the Royal Society about a star so massive that its escape velocity would be greater than the speed of light, so that no light could ever leave it: a "dark star", the first written idea of a black hole.

cecilia-payne-and-the-hydrogen-sun.context_blurb:
What are the stars made of? In 1925 a young Englishwoman at Harvard, Cecilia Payne, answered by reading starlight from hundreds of stars, and her answer was so unexpected that America's leading astronomer called it impossible. She was right.

Payne's road began at Cambridge in December 1919, when she squeezed into a lecture by Arthur Eddington, just back from the African island of Principe. His eclipse expedition there had measured starlight bending around the Sun and so confirmed Einstein's general theory of relativity. That night Payne gave up botany for physics.

Since Cambridge gave women no degrees, she crossed the Atlantic to Harvard with a fellowship. There she studied the spectra of hundreds of stars on glass plates already on the observatory's shelves, plates that Annie Jump Cannon and a team of women "computers" had long sorted by the pattern of dark lines in each star's spectrum.

Her key tool was a 1920 equation by the Indian physicist Meghnad Saha. Astronomers had read a strong spectral line as a sign of plenty of that element, but Saha showed that a line's strength depends mainly on how hot the star's outer layers are, because heat strips electrons from atoms and changes which lines they can make.

Correcting for temperature, Payne found that the Sun and the stars are made mostly of hydrogen, with helium next; together the two lightest elements make up about 98 percent of a star's mass. Her figures raised hydrogen's abundance roughly a millionfold over earlier estimates, and helium's by roughly a thousandfold. Astronomers had pictured stars as built of much the same heavy elements as the Earth. Her thesis earned Harvard's first astronomy doctorate, formally through Radcliffe College because Harvard would not give one to a woman.

The observatory's director, Harlow Shapley, passed her draft to Princeton's Henry Norris Russell, the most powerful astronomer in America, who wrote back that it was clearly impossible for hydrogen to be a million times more abundant than the metals. Afraid her thesis would be rejected, Payne left her calculations standing but inserted one sentence calling the enormous abundance she had derived almost certainly not real. The claim was softened in words, never in the data.

Four years later Russell reached the same answer by a different route. His 1929 study of the solar atmosphere put it at roughly 60 parts hydrogen to 2 of helium, 2 of oxygen, 1 of metallic vapours and 0.8 of free electrons, by volume, and much of the public credit drifted to him.

Payne's hydrogen turned out to hold up two great ideas at once. A Sun made of hydrogen can run on fusion, turning hydrogen into helium, and a hot Big Bang, in which the universe expanded from an early hot, dense state, predicts a cosmos made mostly of those same two lightest elements.

chadwicks-neutron-the-particle-two-great.context_blurb:
In early 1932 James Chadwick, at Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory, found the neutron after about two weeks of almost round-the-clock work. Two other world-class laboratories had the same strange radiation passing through their instruments and called it something it could not have been.

Alpha particles striking beryllium give off a mysterious, penetrating beam. Chadwick aimed it at paraffin wax, which contains carbon and hydrogen, and he chose the wax for its hydrogen, because a hydrogen nucleus is a single proton with nothing else attached. When the beam knocked those protons out of the wax, their recoil speed revealed the beam directly.

The protons flew out far too hard for any kind of light to have pushed them. Using conservation of momentum, Chadwick worked out that the beam must be made of neutral particles about as heavy as protons: neutrons. His letter to Nature, "Possible Existence of a Neutron", appeared in February 1932.

Others had already run the wax test. In January 1932 a Paris team, Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie, Irène being Marie Curie's daughter, had seen the same recoiling protons and blamed gamma rays. They were superb experimenters who won their own Nobel Prize in 1935; their miss came from a wrong assumption about what the radiation had to be.

Chadwick recognised the particle because he had been looking for it for twelve years. His boss at the Cavendish, Ernest Rutherford, had predicted in a Royal Society lecture in 1920 that the nucleus held a neutral particle about the mass of a proton.

The neutron soon opened the atom's heart. Fire a slow proton at uranium and it is pushed away by the nucleus's 92 positive charges, but a neutron carries no electric charge, so nothing repels it until the strong nuclear force grabs it at the surface. In 1938 and 1939 Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann and Lise Meitner used slow neutrons to split uranium.

chance-favors-the-prepared-mind.context_blurb:
"Chance favours the prepared mind" is one of science's favourite sayings, and it has a documented source. Its point is a dry one: preparation usually means an instrument and a habit, a routine check that lets a lucky accident be noticed at all.

Louis Pasteur said it on 7 December 1854, opening a new faculty of sciences for Lille, in northern France, whose students were headed for factories and dye-works: in the fields of observation, he told them, chance helps only a mind that is ready.

His own example was the Danish scientist Ørsted, who noticed, while lecturing in 1820, that a compass needle jerked when current ran through a nearby wire. Anyone could have seen the wobble, but Ørsted had spent years expecting a link between electricity and magnetism, so he grasped what it meant: an electric current makes a magnetic field around the wire.

Preparation can be a scale. On 6 April 1938 the DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett opened a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas and nothing came out. Most people would have assumed a leak, but Plunkett first weighed the whole cylinder on a lab balance and found it as heavy as when full. Sawing it open, he found a slippery white powder inside: Teflon.

Or it can be a habit. Harry Brearley, the Sheffield steel expert, cast a chromium alloy in 1913 that was wrong for the gun barrels he was trying to improve. Because he always polished his samples and etched them with nitric acid, he noticed that this one refused to etch: it was stainless steel.

Sometimes the problem arrives late. In 1968 Spencer Silver of 3M made an adhesive that stuck lightly and peeled off cleanly, and for years he pitched it around the company as a solution waiting for a problem. The problem came when his colleague Art Fry wanted a bookmark for his church hymnal that would not tear the page, and Post-it Notes went on sale in 1980.

A prepared mind is also wary of tidy stories. Newton's falling apple comes from William Stukeley's 1752 memoir, written down about sixty years after the event from a conversation with Newton, and Kekulé's dream of a snake that revealed the benzene ring comes from a speech he gave in 1890, some twenty-five years after publishing the structure. Both are late anecdotes told by the discoverers themselves, not records made at the time. They may be true, but they are testimony, not evidence.

chandrasekhars-limit-and-eddingtons-law-.context_blurb:
When a Sun-like star has burned its fuel, the core left behind becomes a white dwarf: an ember about the size of the Earth holding about as much mass as the Sun. In 1930 a nineteen-year-old Indian physicist, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, found that such embers have a weight limit, and the most famous astrophysicist in the world refused to accept it.

A white dwarf has no fuel left to burn, so heat cannot hold it up. What props it up is a quantum rule, the Pauli exclusion principle, which forbids two electrons from sharing the same state; squeezed together, the electrons push back with a pressure that has nothing to do with temperature.

On the ship from India to England to begin a scholarship at Cambridge, Chandrasekhar added one thing the older theory had left out: special relativity. As the crushed electrons are driven toward the speed of light, their push stops growing fast enough to keep up with gravity. Any white dwarf heavier than roughly 1.4 Suns, he found, has no way to support itself. It must keep collapsing into something even denser, such as a black hole.

In January 1935 Chandrasekhar presented the result at the Royal Astronomical Society in London. He knew from the programme that Arthur Eddington would speak next, but not what he would say, and Eddington attacked the result in front of the room. In The Observatory that year Eddington wrote that there ought to be a law of Nature to stop a star from behaving in so absurd a way. It was a conviction, not a calculation. Chandrasekhar was right, and the limit now carries his name.

Others were already thinking past white dwarfs. Early in 1932, just before Chadwick's discovery of the neutron, the Soviet physicist Landau proposed that a crushed stellar core could act as a single enormous nucleus. Once the neutron was known, he was the first to speculate seriously about a star built entirely of neutrons: a neutron star.

chladnis-sand-figures-making-sound-visib.context_blurb:
Clamp a metal plate at its centre, sprinkle fine sand on it and draw a violin bow down one edge, and the plate sings while the sand draws a picture of the sound. Ernst Chladni, a German physicist and musician, published a book of these shapes in 1787 and toured Europe showing them.

As the plate rings, the sand jumps about and then gathers into crisp, symmetrical lines: stars, rings and six-petalled flowers. You can try it at home with a baking sheet, table salt and a phone speaker.

The sand collects along the lines where the plate is not moving. The plate vibrates in a standing wave, some regions swinging up and down while the lines between them stay still, and the sand is bounced off the moving parts until it comes to rest on those quiet lines. Press a fingertip on the plate while it sounds and the whole pattern rearranges itself around the finger, because the plate cannot vibrate where it is held and must find a new shape that keeps that point still. Robert Hooke had seen a similar effect with flour on glass a century earlier but never followed it up.

In 1831 Michael Faraday tried a far lighter powder, lycopodium spores, and got the reverse: the spores gathered where the plate moved most. The vibrating plate was stirring up tiny currents in the air that swept the spores there, and in a vacuum the reversed pattern does not form.

Inspired by the patterns Chladni had shown Napoleon, the French Academy set a prize in 1809 for a mathematical theory of vibrating plates. The only serious entrant was Sophie Germain, kept out of the École Polytechnique because she was a woman, who taught herself from lecture notes she borrowed. Her first entry was rejected and her second only praised, but in 1816 she won, the first woman to take a grand prize of the Paris Academy. Her winning paper still had errors in its boundary conditions, and Gustav Kirchhoff, later famous for his electrical circuit laws, supplied the correct ones.

Chladni was also bold about rocks from the sky. In 1794 he claimed that the "stones from the sky" described by country people were real visitors from space, and learned men laughed. Then in April 1803 thousands of stones fell on the French village of L'Aigle in broad daylight, in front of hundreds of witnesses, and the investigation that followed, by the physicist Biot, settled it: rocks really do fall to Earth from space.

clair-patterson-the-man-whose-own-lab-wa.context_blurb:
In the early 1950s the American geochemist Clair Patterson tried to measure the age of the Earth and kept getting nonsense. The culprit was lead, which modern life had spread so thickly that it swamped his samples. To get his number he had to build a clean world first, and then he asked where all that lead had come from.

Lead was in his lab's air, its dust, its benches and its glassware, and when he tested his own hair, that held lead too. In 1953 he set up at Caltech one of the earliest ultra-clean laboratories, acid-washing every tool and sealing every door. He would not trust the chemicals his suppliers sent, either: he distilled each one again himself before use.

He ignored the Earth's own rocks, because the planet's surface is endlessly remade by moving plates, weather and hot water, so a rock records only its last reset. Meteorites are debris from the same birth of the Solar System that were never recycled. He chose the Canyon Diablo meteorite, whose fragments, some 30 tonnes of them, lie scattered across northern Arizona because the asteroid exploded on impact about 50,000 years ago and blasted out Meteor Crater.

Every radioactive clock has a weak spot: you must somehow know the starting amount of the decay product, which nobody was around to record. Patterson measured several samples together and plotted them on a straight line, an isochron, and the point where that line crosses the axis gives the starting amount without any guessing. In 1956 he published the age of the Earth as 4.55 billion years, with an uncertainty of 70 million, against roughly 3.3 billion in the textbooks of the day. Today's best value, 4.54 billion, differs from his by only about ten million years.

Then Patterson turned to the lead itself. Nobody had measured the air's lead in 1750 or 1850, so he drilled into the Greenland ice sheet and pulled up a core, in which each year's snow had trapped that year's air and dust before being buried by the next. Read layer by layer, the ice showed lead in recent snow more than two hundred times higher than in the deep layers laid down before industry.

His opponent was no crank. Robert Kehoe, for decades the leading authority on lead in people, ran the Kettering Laboratory in Cincinnati, funded by General Motors, DuPont and the Ethyl Corporation, maker of the leaded petrol additive, and its research was the standard reference. Kehoe held that lead in human bodies was natural, and even that our species had adapted to it. Patterson answered that people had worked lead for only a few thousand years, an instant on the Darwinian scale. He tested the "always there" claim directly. Ancient Peruvian skeletons, about 1,600 years old, held far less lead than modern bone, by a factor of 700 to 1,200, and to rule out the old bone simply leaking, he measured barium and calcium too, which behave like lead in bone and had not shifted.

He kept finding lead where nobody looked. In the late 1960s he showed that canned tuna carried thousands of times more lead than fresh-caught fish, and that the extra came from the lead solder used to seal the seams of the can. His challenges cost him. When the National Research Council formed a panel on airborne lead in 1971, Patterson, the man whose numbers everyone used, was not even invited onto it.

Leaded petrol left American pumps through twenty years of regulation, finished in 1986, but one step mattered most: new cars from 1975 onward carried a catalytic converter, which lead ruins, so they had to burn unleaded fuel. Average blood lead in American children fell from 13.7 micrograms per decilitre in 1976 to 3 by 1991.

clever-hans-the-horse-that-read-faces.context_blurb:
In Berlin in the early 1900s, huge crowds watched a stallion called Clever Hans answer arithmetic questions by tapping his hoof. Nobody was cheating, which is what makes the story so useful: the horse taught psychology how honest people fool themselves, and how to design an experiment that cannot be fooled.

His owner was Wilhelm von Osten, a retired mathematics teacher from a gymnasium, a German secondary school, who trained horses as a hobby, believed animals could learn to reason and charged no admission. Hans's advertised act went far beyond adding small numbers: he did fractions, told the time and spelled out German words, all by taps of the hoof.

In September 1904 a commission that included a vet, a cavalry officer, teachers, a circus man and the head of the Berlin zoo studied the act closely and concluded that there was no trickery at all. They were right. The answer was hidden somewhere they had not thought to look.

Oskar Pfungst, a young psychologist in Berlin, cracked it in 1907 by changing one thing at a time. He varied two conditions independently: whether Hans could see the person asking, and whether that person knew the answer.

The results were stark. When the questioner was visible and knew the answer, Hans got 50 of 56 right, about 89 percent. When Hans could not see the questioner, his score fell to 2 of 35, about 6 percent. The horse's accuracy tracked what the human knew. Watching closely, Pfungst found the signal: as the taps neared the right count, questioners tensed, then gave a tiny upward jerk of the head on the correct tap, and Hans stopped.

Then Pfungst tried a braver test. He took the questioner's place himself, knowing exactly what the cue was, and did his best to hold it back, yet he made the movement anyway without meaning to. That is why von Osten was never caught: the signal was hidden from him too. Sincerity does not protect an experiment.

The lesson still matters. Facilitated communication, in which a helper steadies a non-speaking person's hand over a keyboard, was put to such a test in 1993. When the two were secretly shown different pictures, the typed answer named the picture the facilitator had seen, essentially every time. The facilitators were not lying; like von Osten, they believed. Only a test that kept the helper ignorant of the answer could show it.

clocking-light-jupiters-moons-to-a-mount.context_blurb:
For most of history light seemed to arrive instantly. Measuring its speed took three centuries, from a moon of Jupiter to a mountain in California, and ended not with a better number but with a decision.

Galileo's Two New Sciences of 1638 describes the first attempt: two men with covered lanterns less than a mile apart, one uncovering his lamp and the other answering the moment he sees it. Galileo could not tell whether light took any time at all, only that it must be extraordinarily fast. When Florence's Accademia del Cimento repeated the test in 1667 with lanterns about a mile apart, the delay they were hunting was some eleven millionths of a second, tens of thousands of times too short for human reactions.

The first real measurement came from the sky. Ole Rømer, a Dane working at the Paris Observatory in the 1670s, timed about 140 eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io, which should recur like clockwork every 1.769 days. They came early when the Earth was near Jupiter and late when it was far. In September 1676 he predicted that a coming eclipse would arrive about ten minutes behind the printed tables, and it did. The news appeared that December as an anonymous notice of six paragraphs, written in the third person. Rømer gave no speed. He gave a time, about 22 minutes for light to cross the full width of the Earth's orbit, more than the true 16.6, and Christiaan Huygens later turned it into a speed.

Rømer's boss, Cassini, rejected a finite speed and blamed quirks in the moons' orbits, and Robert Hooke thought the evidence weak. Yet in 1693 Cassini published new eclipse tables with corrections of up to fourteen minutes, set according to where the Earth stood: he used the effect while denying its cause. Isaac Newton squeezed a second discovery from the same eclipses. He asked whether the edge of Jupiter's shadow came out coloured as Io slipped in and out; it did not, so light of every colour must cross space at the same speed.

Proof that the Earth moves came from James Bradley. Between 1725 and 1728 he kept a telescope pointed overhead at a single star, hoping to see parallax, a yearly shift that should peak in June and December. The star did shift, but the biggest swings came in March and September, three months off from where parallax would put them. The famous story, perhaps only a story, says he understood why in 1728 on a boat on the Thames, when the flag at the masthead swung round each time the boat turned, though the wind had not changed. A moving observer must tilt his telescope forward, as a runner tilts an umbrella into falling rain.

In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau brought the measurement down to Earth. He sent a beam from his father's house to a mirror on Montmartre, 8,633 metres away, and back, passing both ways through the gaps of a spinning wheel with 720 teeth. As the wheel sped up, the returning flash vanished at one speed, when a tooth had moved into the gap's place, and came back at twice that speed; the timing gave about 313,000 kilometres a second. On 27 April 1850 Léon Foucault, using a fast-spinning mirror, compared light in air and in water and found it slower in water by a factor of about 1.33, killing the particle theory of light, which had demanded the opposite.

Albert Michelson's rotating mirror on Mount Wilson in 1926 had eight faces and turned 528 times a second, flinging the beam to a reflector on a peak about 35 kilometres off. A speed is only as good as its distance, so surveyors laid invar tape, a metal that barely expands with heat, along the whole line on the ground, one tape length after another.

The chase ended in 1983, when the international conference that governs units simply decided: it made the metre the length of the path light covers in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The speed of light is now exact by definition. One honest loophole remains, because every measurement times a round trip. Nobody has measured light's one-way speed, because to synchronise two far-apart clocks you must already assume the answer.

cold-fusion-1989-the-claim-that-replicat.context_blurb:
On 23 March 1989 two respected electrochemists, Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons, claimed that a glass cell of heavy water on their bench was making nuclear fusion happen at room temperature, a promise of nearly limitless clean energy. Within six weeks the claim was dead, killed not by authority but by replication.

Their first mistake was the setting. They made the announcement to reporters, at a press conference called by the University of Utah, before any paper had been reviewed or any outside lab had seen the data.

Their cell was a rod of palladium, a metal that can absorb several hundred volumes of hydrogen, wired with platinum and sitting in heavy water. Heavy water contains deuterium, hydrogen whose nucleus carries an extra neutron beside its proton. They hoped deuterium packed into the palladium would be squeezed close enough to fuse, and their calorimeter said more heat was coming out than electricity was going in.

Physicists quickly spotted a problem. Real deuterium fusion throws off neutrons, and fusion producing that much heat would have released a flood of them, enough to kill anyone standing beside the cell. The two chemists were alive and well, so their own bodies were evidence against the claim.

Then the world checked. Within weeks more than a hundred laboratories on four continents dropped what they were doing and tried to repeat the experiment. Early positive signals faded as measurements were tightened. At MIT, Richard Petrasso and his colleagues examined the gamma-ray peak the Utah pair had offered as their nuclear fingerprint and found it lacked a Compton edge, the ridge that every genuine peak from that kind of detector shows; it was also narrower than the instrument could produce.

At a meeting of the American Physical Society in Baltimore on 1 May, the Caltech chemist Nathan Lewis reported that his team's careful copy of the cell showed none of the five signs real fusion must leave: excess heat, neutrons, gamma rays, tritium or helium. The claim was effectively over. Why had they rushed? A rival, Steven Jones of Brigham Young University, was preparing his own related paper, and the race to be first, for credit and for patents, pushed Utah to go public a day before the two groups had planned to submit together.

Fleischmann and Pons were never shown to have faked anything; it was error plus haste. A small community still studies excess heat in metals under a new name, low-energy nuclear reactions, though no nuclear mechanism has been demonstrated.

cold-light-glow-sticks-and-luminol.context_blurb:
Fire and light bulbs make light with heat. Some chemical reactions make light with almost none, and you have probably held one: a glow stick. Snapping it breaks a thin glass tube inside so that two solutions mix and release their energy as light.

Test it tonight with two fresh glow sticks. Warmth speeds a reaction and cold slows it, so the stick dropped in hot water blazes brightly and burns out fast, while the one in the freezer glows dimly but lasts for days. The total amount of light is roughly fixed; temperature only decides how fast it is spent.

H. O. Albrecht, a German chemist, found in 1928 that a little-known compound, first made in 1902, gives off a blue glow in alkaline hydrogen peroxide, and that blood speeds the glow. Named luminol in 1934, it became the spray of every crime drama.

Even on a floor washed years ago, luminol picks out old blood in a dim blue shimmer, because the iron held inside haemoglobin molecules survives in tiny residues and sets off the reaction. But blood is not the only trigger. Grated horseradish, rich in a plant enzyme called peroxidase, makes it glow just as brightly, and so can bleach and copper. A luminol glow is a lead for the lab to follow, never a verdict.

cold-spring-harbor-the-office-that-wrote.context_blurb:
The Eugenics Record Office, founded in 1910 at Cold Spring Harbor on New York's Long Island, spent three decades arguing that traits from "feeblemindedness" to crime were inherited, and that the nation should breed them out. It was run by respected scientists on respectable money, and it turned bad science into American law.

Its evidence came from field workers who walked up to strangers' doors in small towns and back roads, notebook in hand, and wrote down each family's supposed "defects" on cards. Its founder, Davenport, was a Harvard-trained biologist, and its money came from the most admired donors in America: Mary Harriman, widow of a railroad fortune, the Rockefeller Foundation and the Carnegie Institution. The policy it pushed hardest was forced sterilization of the people it labelled unfit.

Its superintendent, Harry Laughlin, went beyond papers. In 1922 he published a Model Eugenical Sterilization Law, ready-made statute language that a legislature could adopt almost unchanged, naming nine categories of people from the "feeble-minded" to the "indigent". Virginia's 1924 law, upheld by the Supreme Court in Buck v. Bell, was built on it, and by the mid-1930s roughly 18 other states had passed laws based on his template. By 1956 more than 59,000 Americans had been sterilized.

He also shaped immigration law. Testifying three times before a House committee between 1920 and 1924, Laughlin used pedigree charts to argue that some nationalities carried "defective stock", and the 1924 Johnson-Reed Act set immigration quotas by national origin. His statistics were later shown to be flawed.

The end came from inside. A visiting committee from the Carnegie Institution examined the office's science in 1935 and judged the work seriously wanting, mostly second- or third-rate. Vannevar Bush, Carnegie's new president, acted in 1939: he forced Laughlin out and closed the office.

Laughlin's later years speak for themselves. In 1936 the University of Heidelberg in Nazi Germany gave him an honorary degree, honouring him for "the science of racial cleansing", in the words of its citation, and he accepted by mail. The next year, with money from the textile heir Wickliffe Draper, he helped found the Pioneer Fund and became its first president. Its first project was to show Erbkrank ("The Hereditary Defective"), a propaganda film made by the Nazi regime, in American schools and churches.

copernicuss-deathbed-book.context_blurb:
In the spring of 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish cathedral canon, lay dying after a stroke, and by the recorded account a printed copy of his book reached him on his last day. He had held it back for nearly thirty years. It made the Earth one of six planets travelling round a Sun that stands still, while spinning daily on its own axis.

The new picture explained a puzzle of the night sky. Mars usually drifts eastward against the stars, but every couple of years it slows, stops and loops backward for about seventy days. Copernicus's answer is that the Earth, on the faster inside track, is overtaking Mars, which then seems to slide backward, as a slower car does when you pass it. You can watch it yourself: the next loop runs from about January to April 2027.

Copernicus was no great observer. Busy with cathedral duties at Frombork, he recorded perhaps twenty-seven observations of his own, and built his book on centuries-old records from Ptolemy and from the Islamic astronomer al-Battani. What drove him was a flaw in Ptolemy's system, a device called the equant: an off-centre point from which each planet appeared to sweep at an even rate, though it moved unevenly about the true centre of its own circle. To Copernicus it broke the very rule of uniform circular motion it was meant to serve.

In 1539 a young mathematician, Rheticus, came to study with him, the only pupil Copernicus ever had, and in 1540 he printed a short summary of the theory, the Narratio Prima, or "First Narration". When the full book went to press at Nuremberg in 1543, the Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander slipped in an unsigned preface, placed before Copernicus's own dedication, telling readers that the hypotheses did not have to be true, nor even likely, as long as the calculations matched the sky. Copernicus had argued the opposite. In 1609 Johannes Kepler proved who wrote the preface, from a handwritten note in Hieronymus Schreiber's copy of the book.

The new system was not more accurate. Copernicus kept perfect circles and still needed dozens of extra ones, and his predictions were about as good as Ptolemy's, within roughly ten arcminutes. Its gain was structure: the planets fell into one order and the backward loops came out naturally. Nor was the idea wholly new. Aristarchus of Samos had placed the Sun at the centre some eighteen centuries earlier, and Copernicus mentioned him in an early manuscript, then struck the passage out before the book went to press.

Rome let the book be for 73 years; it bore a dedication to the Pope, and Jesuit colleges taught it. It was suspended "until corrected" only in 1616, when Galileo was pressing heliocentrism as physical fact. The correction, in 1620, named nine sentences to be cut or reworded. Arthur Koestler later called it the book nobody read, but Owen Gingerich went and looked: over three decades he hunted down first editions, and his 2002 census of 277 copies found many thick with the working notes of sixteenth-century astronomers.

The great objection was the stars. If the Earth swung around a vast orbit, nearby stars should shift a little every six months, and Tycho Brahe, whose instruments were good to about one arcminute, saw no shift. That pushed the stars so far away that, by his measurement of their apparent size, each ordinary star would have to be as wide as the Earth's whole orbit, which he took as absurd. Proof that the Earth moves came in 1728, when James Bradley and Samuel Molyneux, hunting that shift, found every star displaced the same odd way: starlight arrives tilted because the observer is racing through space. The shift itself waited until 1838, when Friedrich Bessel chose 61 Cygni, a star Giuseppe Piazzi had seen racing across the sky. Nearby stars slide fastest against the distant ones behind them, so a fast mover was a good bet to be close, and Bessel measured its shift at about a third of an arcsecond.

correlation-is-not-causation.context_blurb:
When two things rise and fall together, it is tempting to think one causes the other. Often it does not: a hidden third thing may drive both, the arrow may point the other way, or the link may be pure coincidence. Telling these apart is one of the most useful skills in science, and even great scientists have failed at it.

In a beach town, ice-cream sales and drownings climb on the same days. The ice cream is not drowning anyone: hot weather sends people both to the ice-cream counter and into the water. A hidden factor that drives two others together is called a confounder. Likewise, children with bigger shoes read better, but not because of the shoes: older children simply have bigger feet and are stronger readers. Compare only eight-year-olds with eight-year-olds and the pattern disappears.

In 2000 the statistician Robert Matthews made the point with a joke paper, "Storks Deliver Babies". Across 17 European countries, the number of breeding stork pairs really did track the number of births, until he took account of how big each country is: larger countries simply have more of both. Sometimes the arrow runs backwards. In the Middle Ages people saw that the sick carried few lice and concluded that lice were good for health. In fact illness brought fever, and lice abandon a body that grows too hot. That is reverse causation.

Confounders fool professionals too. Richard Stone and Graham Quinn alarmed new parents in 1999 with a Nature paper linking night lights in babies' rooms to nearsightedness. Follow-up studies in 2000, one led by Karla Zadnik and one by Jane Gwiazda, found the hidden factor: nearsighted parents were the ones more likely to leave night lights on, and nearsightedness runs in families. The strongest defence is randomization. When a coin flip decides who gets a treatment, the link between the treatment and every other trait of the patients is cut, so income, habits and health balance out between the groups.

With enough data, coincidences are guaranteed. The software developer Tyler Vigen collects unrelated series that move together; his most famous pairs American cheese eating with deaths from getting tangled in bedsheets, matched almost perfectly over ten years.

For years doctors advised hormone therapy after menopause to protect the heart, because women taking it had fewer heart attacks. Then on 9 July 2002 the Women's Health Initiative, a large randomized trial, was halted early: the women given combined estrogen plus progestin had more heart disease, strokes and blood clots than those given a placebo. The earlier studies had been fooled by healthy-user bias, because the women who chose the therapy were already healthier and wealthier.

The great statistician who pioneered randomized experiments was fooled too. Ronald Fisher insisted in the late 1950s that smoking might not cause lung cancer, blaming instead a shared genetic constitution that produced both the urge to smoke and the disease. Fisher was a heavy pipe smoker and a paid consultant to the tobacco industry, and he was wrong. The proof came without forcing anyone to smoke. Austin Bradford Hill and Richard Doll surveyed every doctor in Britain in 1951 and followed some 40,000 of them for decades. The most telling result was a dose-response curve: the more the doctors smoked, the higher their risk, and the risk fell when they quit.

counting-the-thunder-measuring-the-speed.context_blurb:
A thunderstorm hands you a free experiment: see the flash, count until the bang. For four centuries people turned that gap into a measurement of the speed of sound, and the story is full of clever tricks for beating the wind, the clock and their own mistakes.

Light from the flash arrives almost instantly, but sound plods along at about 343 metres a second, so the seconds you count are the sound's journey. Every three seconds of counting means about one kilometre of distance, or five seconds a mile. Beyond about 16 kilometres the thunder usually fades and the count never ends.

Thunder itself is made by heat. A lightning channel reaches about 30,000 degrees, roughly five times as hot as the surface of the Sun, and the air blasts outward faster than sound in a shock wave that becomes the bang. A strike right overhead is one sharp crack. A distant bolt rumbles for many seconds because it is kilometres of crooked path: sound from the nearest part reaches you first and sound from the far end arrives seconds later.

Sound's speed depends on what it travels through. In helium it runs about three times faster than in air, so after a lungful of balloon gas the hollow spaces of the throat and mouth resonate at higher notes and the voice squeaks, though the vocal cords buzz exactly as before. In liquids and solids it is faster still: about 1,500 metres a second in water, 5,000 in steel and 12,000 in diamond, but only about 50 in soft rubber. The fast materials resist being squeezed with enormous force, and that stiffness outweighs their extra density.

Air pressure does not change the speed, because denser air and higher pressure cancel exactly. Temperature does: sound gains about 0.6 metres a second for every degree Celsius. On a hot August afternoon the thunder reaches you sooner, so a plain three-seconds-per-kilometre count puts the storm a little closer than it really is.

The first good measurements needed a better clock. Early attempts timed cannon against a free-swinging pendulum, one eye on the pendulum and one on the distant flash, and came out far too fast. In 1708 William Derham, a parson in Upminster, Essex, listened from his church tower for guns firing twelve miles off, timing them with a pendulum clock whose tick he could hear every half second, so both his eyes stayed on the muzzle flash. Even then he did not trust his figure. He walked six miles of dark tidal sands on the Essex coast, firing muskets at nearly every mile, at real risk from the sea and the night, and the shots confirmed his earlier results.

Wind was the other enemy: a tailwind speeds sound up and a headwind slows it. In 1738 a French team firing cannon along a line about 28 kilometres long fired from both ends and averaged the two runs, so the wind's push in one direction cancelled its drag in the other. They found 337 metres a second, day or night, rain or shine.

In October 1826 Jean-Daniel Colladon took the question under Lake Geneva. He struck a bell beneath one boat while setting off a flash of gunpowder, and listened from another about 13 kilometres away. With his head under water he could hear only about two kilometres, so he built a listening tube, five metres of tin, closed at the bottom and full of air, through which the distant bell rang clearly. The answer was 1,435 metres a second in fresh water, almost exactly what he had calculated beforehand.

Theory lagged behind. In his Principia of 1687 Isaac Newton calculated the speed from the pressure and density of air and got about 295 metres a second, roughly a sixth too slow. Once Derham's numbers left no room for doubt, Newton patched his theory in later editions with corrections for the thickness of air's particles and for its moisture; the historian R. S. Westfall later called the fudge nothing short of deliberate fraud. Pierre-Simon Laplace located the real error in 1816. Air warms when it is squeezed, and a sound wave passes too quickly for that warmth to escape, so the air springs back stiffer than Newton assumed.

counting-the-uncountable-avogadros-numbe.context_blurb:
Chemists weigh things in grams but think in particles, and linking the two meant counting atoms no one could see. The count is now known exactly, but the path to it ran through an ignored Italian, a famous congress and a ball of silicon polished almost beyond belief.

The chemist's counting unit is the mole: about 602,000 billion billion particles. It is a number too big to picture, yet one mole of water, about 18 grams, is roughly a single tablespoon.

The idea that made counting possible came from Amedeo Avogadro in 1811: equal volumes of any two gases, under identical temperature and pressure, hold the same number of molecules. A jar and a thermometer became a way to compare counts.

His idea lay neglected for nearly fifty years while chemists quarrelled over atomic weights. At the first international chemistry congress, at Karlsruhe in 1860, Stanislao Cannizzaro handed out a pamphlet reviving Avogadro's rule, and the chemists left with an agreed, consistent set of atomic weights. Mendeleev was there and later said it cleared his head. Avogadro had died four years before, unrecognised.

Avogadro never measured the count himself. In 1865 the physicist Loschmidt used the kinetic theory of gases, combining the size of a molecule with the average distance a molecule flies before it hits another. The name Avogadro's number was attached later by Jean Perrin, so the man it honours never held a number.

Today the count is fixed by definition, but the work behind it was extraordinary. An international team made one-kilogram spheres of almost pure silicon-28 so round that, if one were enlarged until it matched our planet, the highest bump would stand only a few metres tall. They measured each sphere's volume with light and the spacing of its atoms with X-rays, and so counted the atoms inside.

cracking-the-code-nirenbergs-poly-u.context_blurb:
By the late 1950s biologists knew that DNA's four-letter alphabet spells out proteins built from twenty amino acids, but nobody had read a single word of the language. In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei, working at America's NIH, read the first one, using a message no living thing had ever written.

The physicist George Gamow, of Big Bang fame, had the arithmetic right in 1954: four letters taken three at a time give sixty-four words, plenty for twenty amino acids. But his picture of how the code is read missed almost entirely. He pictured amino acids slotting directly into diamond-shaped pockets between the bases of the DNA double helix itself. To crack the code he founded the RNA Tie Club, twenty members for the twenty amino acids, each with a black wool tie and a gold tiepin engraved with the three-letter abbreviation of his own amino acid. Its real work travelled in memos, including Francis Crick's 1955 idea of a small adaptor molecule, later found to be transfer RNA.

In the small hours of 27 May 1961 Matthaei ran twenty tubes side by side, each holding ground-up bacteria still able to make protein, with all twenty amino acids but a different one made radioactive in each tube. Into every tube went the same artificial RNA, a chain of nothing but uracil. Only the phenylalanine tube built protein: UUU spells phenylalanine, the first word of the genetic code ever read. A second tube made the result believable. It held everything except the artificial RNA and gave 70 counts against 38,000, answering the worry that the broken bacteria were simply reading messages of their own.

In August 1961 Nirenberg, unknown outside his corridor, read the result to about thirty-five people at an international biochemistry congress in Moscow. When word reached Francis Crick, Crick arranged for Nirenberg to give the whole talk again before the full congress, to more than a thousand listeners. A race followed against the famous laboratory of Severo Ochoa, a Nobel winner, and in what was later called the NIH's finest hour, scientists across the institute set their own projects aside to work for Nirenberg. In 1968 he became the first federal employee to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Meanwhile Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner and their colleagues showed how the words are read. Using a dye that slips extra bases into a virus gene, they found that a single added base ruined the protein, two still ruined it, but three restored it: the letters further along were grouped into the same three-letter words as before. So the code is read three letters at a time, without overlaps, from a set starting point.

Reading one word at a time by watching protein form was slow. Nirenberg and Philip Leder's 1964 shortcut was faster: combine ribosomes, one short RNA triplet and amino-acid-loaded transfer RNAs, some radioactive, then filter the mix through nitrocellulose. The sheet catches ribosomes, while transfer RNA that has not docked runs straight through, so radioactivity on the sheet means a match. Har Gobind Khorana confirmed the dictionary by a different route: he built RNA messages to order, in any repeating pattern he chose, and read the same code back out of them. By 1966 the table was complete, with three stop words that name no amino acid. The first, amber, was named by Richard Epstein and Charles Steinberg after their friend Harris Bernstein, whose surname is German for amber.

The code has spare capacity, and it is spent unevenly: leucine has six words, tryptophan only one. About seventy percent of single-letter changes that leave the amino acid unchanged land on the third letter of a word, which pairs loosely with transfer RNA, as Crick's 1966 wobble idea explained. That slack makes the code forgiving of typos. And bacteria, oak trees, whales and people all read essentially the same table, with only small variations, among the strongest evidence that every living thing descends from one common ancestor. More than thirty natural variants are known, so the honest phrase is nearly universal.

crispr-came-out-of-a-yogurt-factory.context_blurb:
The most powerful gene-editing tool of our time was not invented. It was found inside bacteria, as part of their defence against viruses, by researchers who were not looking for a tool at all: a Spanish microbiologist, a yogurt company and two women who went on to win a Nobel Prize.

Bacteria get infected by viruses called phages, which inject their DNA and take the cell over. Many bacteria keep a record of past attackers: short pieces of phage DNA filed between repeating stretches of their own DNA. Biologists named that file CRISPR, after the pattern of short, regularly spaced repeats it makes in the DNA. Francisco Mojica in Spain realised that the filed pieces were viral, the microbe's memory of old enemies, and four leading journals rejected his paper.

The proof came from industry. Danisco, a supplier of starter cultures for yogurt and cheese, kept losing vats of bacteria to bacteriophages, the viruses that attack bacteria. Its researchers Barrangou and Horvath infected Streptococcus thermophilus with a phage and sequenced the bacteria that survived. Each survivor had added a new spacer, a fresh entry matching that exact phage, to its CRISPR file. By adding or deleting spacers by hand they could switch resistance on and off, and they published in Science in 2007.

Gene editing already existed, but it was slow. The main editing tool of that decade, zinc-finger nucleases, needed a fresh custom-built cutting protein for every new DNA target, which could take months of protein engineering. CRISPR would need only a new strand of RNA.

Emmanuelle Charpentier, a French microbiologist studying the strep-throat germ Streptococcus pyogenes, found in 2011 that its cutting protein, Cas9, needs a second small RNA, tracrRNA, without which it will not cut DNA at all. She met Jennifer Doudna at a conference in Puerto Rico, and in August 2012 the two published the trick that made CRISPR a tool for any laboratory: they joined the two natural RNAs into one single guide RNA that a scientist can write to match any 20-letter target. A team in Lithuania reached a similar result independently and was turned away by the journal Cell.

Why doesn't a bacterium shred its own file, which is also viral DNA? Cas9 cuts only where a short tag, the PAM, sits right beside the target. The copies stored in the bacterium's own chromosome have no PAM next to them, so Cas9 passes its own records by.

In 2020 Charpentier and Doudna shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first science Nobel ever awarded to two women alone.
