cure-or-enhance-where-the-germline-line-.context_blurb:
Gene editing can change two very different kinds of cells. Edit an adult patient's body cells, with her consent, and the change ends with her. Edit an embryo, and the change runs through every cell of a person who could not be asked, and on through every generation after. Nearly every argument in the field turns on that difference.

Scientists have paused before. At Asilomar, on the California coast, in February 1975, researchers, lawyers and journalists drew up safety rules for recombinant DNA, the new technique of joining genes from different species. The biologists had already halted their own work while the rules were written: a voluntary pause of this kind is called a moratorium.

When the world's science academies first met on human gene editing, in Washington in December 2015 under David Baltimore's chairmanship, they concluded that it would be irresponsible to go ahead with any clinical use of edited embryos until the safety and ethical questions were settled and society broadly agreed. Three years later one researcher ignored them. He Jiankui told a Hong Kong summit in November 2018 that he had used CRISPR to edit the embryos of twin girls, now born; he had bypassed ethics review and forged approvals, and a court in Shenzhen jailed him for three years.

Enhancement also fails as science. In 2019 Karavani and colleagues simulated choosing, from a batch of IVF embryos, the one with the best genetic score for IQ. The average gain was only about 2.5 IQ points, because each of thousands of gene variants contributes only a tiny amount, and many variants affect several traits at once: some that push IQ up also push up the risk of anorexia.

The rules on human experiments were written in answer to scandal. In 1972 Peter Buxtun, a Public Health Service worker, took to the Associated Press what he knew of the Tuskegee syphilis study, which had run since 1932. The outcry produced a new federal law in 1974 and the Belmont Report of 1979, resting on three principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

dalton-weighs-the-invisible-and-wills-hi.context_blurb:
John Dalton, a largely self-taught Quaker schoolmaster in Manchester, ran two lifelong experiments. One turned atoms from an ancient Greek guess into things a chemist could weigh. The other used his own eyes, which saw colours differently, and he willed them to science to settle what was wrong with them.

Dalton's 1808 book gave each element a symbol, a little circle carrying its own sign: hydrogen a central dot, nitrogen a single upright bar, and oxygen a plain ring with nothing in it at all. For the metals he put the first letter of the metal's name inside the circle: C for copper, L for lead, G for gold. Jöns Jacob Berzelius later dropped the circles and kept the letters, which is why chemists now write Fe and Cu.

Dalton did not invent the atom; Democritus had imagined it two thousand years earlier. What his 1808 book carried that had never existed before was a table of the relative weights of the atoms, which turned speculation into something you could check on a balance. His evidence was whole numbers. Burning carbon two different ways gives two gases, now named carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, and for the same weight of carbon, one gas held exactly twice as much oxygen as the other. Exactly twice, never anything in between: whole numbers mean separate lumps.

His atomic weights rested on a guess. No one could see a molecule, so for water Dalton used his rule of greatest simplicity: when two elements form only one compound, assume one atom of each. Water came out as one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom, HO rather than H2O, and his weight for oxygen was about half the true figure. Around 1810 the engineer Peter Ewart made him wooden balls with holes for pegs, so he could build compounds in three dimensions, the forerunners of classroom ball-and-stick models. Dalton confessed in 1842 to one deliberate untruth in them: every ball was the same size, though he knew atoms differ, because matching balls taught better.

Dalton's other experiment was himself. He once gave his mother stockings he believed were a sober Quaker blue, and she asked what had made him choose such a bright colour: they were scarlet. That is family legend, and so is another story: asked by William Whewell at Cambridge what his scarlet doctor's gown looked like, Dalton pointed at the leaves of the trees. On 31 October 1794 he read the first scientific report on colour blindness to a Manchester society, and the eyes he described were his own.

He set down exactly what he saw: scarlet looked to him like green, and pink like blue. The most important line in the paper was that his brother confused exactly the same pairs, so the trait ran in the family, decades before anyone knew of genes. Dalton also offered an explanation he thought almost beyond doubt: the jelly-like fluid filling his eyeball must be tinted blue, filtering out red. It was a good hypothesis, specific and testable, and he asked that his eyes be examined after his death.

Dalton died on 27 July 1844, and the next day his physician Joseph Ransome opened one eye. The fluid was perfectly clear, with no tint at all. Dalton's theory had failed Dalton's own test. Ransome then sliced the back off the second eye and looked through it like a lens: red and green came through in their true colours, so the fault lay not in the eye's fluids but somewhere behind them.

His eyes were kept in a jar in Manchester. In 1995 D. M. Hunt, J. D. Mollon and colleagues extracted DNA from tissue preserved for 150 years and found that the gene for the green-sensitive pigment was missing entirely: Dalton was a deuteranope. Thomas Young, working only from Dalton's descriptions, had judged that he lacked red-sensitive receptors, a verdict that stood for nearly two centuries until molecular biology corrected it.

dart-the-first-time-humans-deliberately-.context_blurb:
On 26 September 2022, NASA ran an experiment that had been only theory for decades: it deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid to see whether it could shift it. The mission was DART, the Double Asteroid Redirection Test, and its target was Dimorphos, a moonlet about 160 metres wide circling a larger asteroid, Didymos.

The roughly 500-kilogram craft struck at about 22,500 kilometres an hour, photographing the rock right up to the moment of impact. The aim was to show that we can push an asteroid off its course by ramming it.

Despite talk of planetary defence, no rock was knocked away from Earth. Neither Didymos nor Dimorphos was ever on a course to hit our planet; the pair was chosen precisely because it was safe, and because it could be measured. DART changed only Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos, not the pair's path around the Sun.

Dimorphos circles Didymos about every 12 hours, passing in front of it, so telescopes on Earth can time its orbit by the dimming. Before the impact NASA set the bar for success: the orbit had to shrink by at least 73 seconds. Choosing that threshold beforehand is what separated a genuine test from storytelling after the fact.

The orbit actually shortened by about half an hour, some 32 to 33 minutes, more than twenty times the bar. Simple momentum from the spacecraft alone should have shortened it by only about 7 minutes. Most of the extra push came from the debris: the crash blasted a plume of pulverised rock off the surface, and as it streamed away in one direction it shoved Dimorphos the other way, like a rocket's exhaust. Scientists put that boost at about 3.6 times the spacecraft's own push.

No human could steer the final approach: a radio signal took over a minute to go to Earth and back, and the moonlet only became visible in the final hour. Software on board, called SMART Nav, picked Dimorphos out of the camera images and steered the spacecraft into it automatically.

How hard a crash pushes depends on what the asteroid is made of, which is still poorly known. So in October 2024 the European Space Agency launched Hera, due to arrive in late 2026 to examine the crater and find Dimorphos's true mass, turning a one-off demonstration into a calibrated tool.

darwins-finches-the-birds-he-misfiled.context_blurb:
The Galapagos finches are biology's most famous story, and the usual version is wrong in several places. Charles Darwin did not grasp evolution while studying their beaks on the islands; he mislabelled them, lost track of where they came from, and understood them only later, with other people's help. The real proof of evolution in these birds came 140 years later, from two scientists with calipers.

HMS Beagle was away from England for nearly five years, but she spent only about five weeks at the Galapagos, in September and October 1835, and Darwin was ashore for about nineteen days. He collected many small, dull-coloured birds and labelled them as he thought they were: wrens, blackbirds and grosbeaks, unrelated common kinds. He also mostly failed to record their islands. The historian Frank Sulloway found that Darwin's Ornithological Notes give a locality for only three of his 31 finches.

What did catch his eye were the mockingbirds, whose island of origin he had noted for each specimen: those from Charles Island, from Albemarle, and from James and Chatham were three different kinds. Hearing too from the vice-governor, Nicholas Lawson, that the tortoises differed from island to island, Darwin wrote privately in 1835 that if there was any foundation for such remarks, such facts would undermine the notion that species are fixed. He published nothing like it for more than twenty years.

The insight arrived in London. In January 1837 the ornithologist John Gould reported that Darwin's wrens, blackbirds and grosbeaks belonged to a single family of closely related ground finches, which forced Darwin to ask how one group of birds could come to differ so much between islands. To rebuild the missing island data he borrowed carefully labelled birds from three shipmates: Captain Robert FitzRoy, FitzRoy's steward Harry Fuller, and Darwin's own servant, Syms Covington. Even in 1845, in the second edition of his Journal, he wrote only that one might really fancy a single original species had been changed to serve different purposes.

Even the name is not Darwin's. The ornithologist Percy Lowe coined "Darwin's finches" in 1935, in a paper concluding that the birds were a confusing swarm showing no clear sign of new species forming. David Lack's 1947 book made the name famous and reversed that verdict. And DNA read in the early 2000s showed they are not finches at all: all 18 species belong to the tanager family, descended from a single seed-eater that arrived from South America a million or two years ago.

Peter and Rosemary Grant began work on the bare volcanic islet of Daphne Major in 1973 and returned year after year for four decades, trapping, banding and measuring the beaks of almost every finch on the island with calipers. In 1977 the rains failed and about 85 percent of the medium ground finches starved. The survivors had deeper beaks, because the only food left was the hard, spiny seed cases of the puncture vine, which a shallow beak cannot crack. Average beak depth rose from 9.2 to about 9.9 millimetres in one generation, and when floods in 1982 and 1983 brought back small seeds, selection swung the other way. Then in 1981 a single male cactus finch flew over 100 kilometres from Española and bred with the residents. Within three generations his line had stopped breeding with the locals, kept apart by song and beak size: a new species forming before the scientists' eyes.

Evolution on the islands produced stranger habits too. On the remote, waterless islands of Wolf and Darwin, a small ground finch was seen in 1964 jabbing at a nesting booby until it bled, then drinking the blood. Researchers think the habit grew out of cleaning parasites from the boobies' skin.

davos-schwab-the-great-reset-and-the-sen.context_blurb:
Every January presidents, billionaires and business chiefs meet at the World Economic Forum in a Swiss ski resort. Its most quoted sentences are often pinned on the wrong people, so the useful skill here is checking who actually said what, where and in what form. The honest criticism needs no myths: the Forum convenes people with real power, in public, with no voters behind it.

It began in January 1971, when Klaus Schwab, then teaching at Geneva's university, invited about 450 European business leaders to a two-week "European Management Symposium" in Davos, the town whose name the yearly gathering still carries. Schwab is often called a banker, but he is not one: he holds doctorates in engineering, from ETH Zurich, and in economics, from the University of Fribourg.

The line most often hung on the Forum, a city dweller in 2030 owning nothing and having no privacy yet happier than ever, came from no secret plan, and Schwab never wrote it. It headed an imaginative essay about life in 2030, published by the Forum in November 2016 and written by Ida Auken, a member of the Danish parliament. After it spread and drew fierce criticism, Auken added a note saying the piece was one possible scenario, meant to get people debating what technology might bring, good and bad, and the Forum gave it a new title.

Schwab's own ideas are signed and can be quoted exactly. In January 2016 he used the Davos meeting to launch his book The Fourth Industrial Revolution, arguing that the physical, digital and biological worlds were fusing and would need new forms of governance. On 9 July 2020, with Thierry Malleret, he published COVID-19: The Great Reset, presenting the pandemic as an opening to rebuild economies around stakeholder capitalism and closer partnership between governments and business. Because they are books anyone can buy, criticism of them can be precise.

Rumours deserve the same checking. A story spread online that Schwab's father, Eugen, was a Nazi Party member and a confidant of Hitler. Historians and fact-checkers found no evidence that he was a party member; he managed a plant in Ravensburg for the Swiss engineering firm Escher Wyss. A criticism you can document is worth more than one you cannot.

davys-battery-tears-new-metals-out-of-ro.context_blurb:
Humphry Davy, the star chemist of London's Royal Institution, made himself his own first experiment and then used the biggest battery of his age to tear new metals out of rock. Along the way he named a gas, broke a famous rule of chemistry, saved miners' lives and hired the assistant who would outshine him.

In 1799, at Thomas Beddoes's Pneumatic Institution in Bristol, the twenty-year-old Davy inhaled nitrous oxide over 160 times between April and June, logging his own racing pulse and fits of laughter, and gave it the name it still carries: laughing gas. On Boxing Day that year he sealed himself in an airtight box built by James Watt, the steam-engine pioneer, and breathed the gas for over an hour. Davy noticed it eased the pain of his inflamed gums, and in his book of 1800 he suggested it might be used in surgery. Surgeons ignored the hint and went on operating on conscious patients for some forty more years.

In October 1807 Davy passed the current of a huge battery of copper and zinc plates, 274 in all, through melted potash, a fierce alkali from wood ash that no one had ever split. Bright silvery globules formed and burst into flame as they reached the surface. According to his cousin and assistant, Edmund Davy, recalling it years later, Humphry danced around the room with joy and needed time to calm down before he could continue. The new metal was potassium. Dropped into water, a globule caught fire with a lilac flame and floated on the surface as it burned, because it is lighter than water. No furnace or charcoal could have freed it, because the metal clings to its oxygen too tightly; the current tore the oxygen away by sheer electrical force, dragging it to the other wire. Sodium followed, and in 1808 calcium, magnesium, strontium, barium and boron.

The earths of 1808 fought back: his current freed each metal and lost it again at once. Berzelius, in Sweden, wrote with the fix: pass the current through the lime into a pool of mercury, which absorbs the new metal as it forms. Davy then boiled the mercury away and held the pure metal. The trick was Berzelius's, not Davy's.

In 1810 Davy struck at the great Antoine Lavoisier. Try as he might, he could pull no oxygen out of the greenish-yellow gas then called oxymuriatic gas; it was an element, which he named chlorine. That meant muriatic acid, a classic strong acid, held no oxygen at all. It broke Lavoisier's rule that oxygen makes acids, a rule built into the very name oxygen, from Greek roots meaning acid-former.

An explosion of nitrogen trichloride injured his eyes in November 1812. Unable to write for months while his eyes recovered, he hired a helper in March 1813: a young bookbinder's apprentice who had attended his lectures and sent him a hand-bound book of notes on them, Michael Faraday.

Coal miners' lamps were naked flames, and the mines held firedamp, or methane, so the light they needed could blow them up. Testing flames in the autumn of 1815, Davy found that a flame cannot pass through fine wire gauze, because the metal wires draw heat out of the burning gas faster than the fire can spread, cooling it below the point where methane ignites. So he wrapped an oil flame in a tube of fine metal mesh. Gas could drift in and burn safely inside, and the caged flame became a gas detector: when firedamp rose, it stretched taller and burned blue. Davy never patented the lamp and let anyone copy it for free, saying his only aim had been to serve humanity.

defining-a-temperature-and-finding-its-f.context_blurb:
Before thermometers agreed with each other, two people in two cities could not know whether their "hot" meant the same thing. Making temperature a number anyone could share took better instruments, careful definitions and the discovery of a floor below which nothing can be cooled.

Fahrenheit's greatest gift was not his scale but his hardware: around 1721 he perfected the mercury-in-glass thermometer, reliable enough that readings taken by strangers in different places meant the same thing. Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer, anchored his 1742 scale to the points where water freezes and where it boils. Because water boils at a lower temperature where the air pressure is lower, as on a mountain, he specified boiling at the mean barometric pressure found at sea level. His scale was first published upside down and turned the right way up within a year.

Gases pointed to a floor. Seal any gas in a rigid vessel, cool it and plot its pressure against temperature, and you get a falling straight line. Oxygen, nitrogen and helium each give a line, and extended downward, they all meet at a single point on the temperature axis, where the pressure would be zero. In 1848 William Thomson proposed making that point the zero of an absolute scale, now measured in kelvins: about minus 273 degrees Celsius.

Absolute zero is not where all motion stops, as schoolbooks often say. The uncertainty principle forbids any particle from being perfectly still, so even at zero kelvin some zero-point energy always remains: it is the lowest possible energy, not zero energy. Nor can it be reached. Walther Nernst's third law of thermodynamics, from 1906, says no finite number of steps gets there, because every cooling method removes only a fraction of the heat that is left at each step. Halve, halve and halve again, and you never arrive.

The race toward the floor has produced wonders. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes first turned helium into a liquid at Leiden on 10 July 1908, at about 4 kelvin; three years later, mercury chilled in it lost all electrical resistance, the discovery of superconductivity. Researchers in Bremen in 2021 let a cloud of rubidium atoms fall through a 122-metre drop tower and, during the fall, held it at about 38 picokelvin, 38 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero. And since 20 May 2019 the kelvin itself has been defined not by a cell of pure water but by fixing an exact value for a constant of nature, the Boltzmann constant.

deutsche-physik-a-state-decides-which-ph.context_blurb:
In 1930s Germany two Nobel Prize-winning physicists campaigned to throw Einstein's relativity out of the universities as "Jewish physics", and the Nazi state gave them the power to enforce it. The movement called itself Deutsche Physik, German Physics, and it shows what happens when a government decides which science is allowed.

Its leaders were Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark, both German Nobel laureates in physics. In the foreword to his four-volume textbook Deutsche Physik, published in Munich in 1936 and 1937, Lenard wrote that science, like everything people create, is determined by race and blood.

The state supplied the muscle. On 7 April 1933 the Nazi government passed the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which removed from universities and offices anyone with a Jewish grandparent or a record of opposing the Nazis. By 1938 roughly a quarter of Germany's physicists had lost their posts, and eleven past or future Nobel laureates, among them Max Born and James Franck, had left the country. Stark was made president of the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt, the national standards institute, and also ran the main research-funding body, giving him control over jobs and money across German physics.

Ancestry was never the real test. In July 1937 Stark used Das Schwarze Korps, the newspaper of the SS, to brand Werner Heisenberg, a non-Jewish German, a "white Jew" for teaching the new theoretical physics and defending relativity. In 1936 Heisenberg had answered the movement with a petition signed by German physics professors, drawn up with Hans Geiger, of the Geiger counter, and Max Wien. Their argument was practical: abstract theory, such as Maxwell's equations, is what gave the world radio.

Heisenberg was saved not by argument but by family connections. Heisenberg's mother knew Himmler's mother and made her appeal there, and in July 1938 Heinrich Himmler cleared him on one condition: he could teach relativity so long as he never named Einstein. Open defiance was rare. On 18 September 1933, opening the German Physical Society's meeting at Würzburg, Max von Laue compared the attack on relativity to the Church's silencing of Galileo and closed with the words legend gives Galileo, "Eppur si muove", "and yet it moves".

In the end Deutsche Physik failed on its own terms. A physics that rejected relativity and quantum mechanics could not compute a nuclear reaction, and the people who could, Born, Franck, Bethe, Meitner and many others, had been driven out, handing the lead in theoretical physics to Britain and the United States.

dewars-flask-and-the-three-roads-heat-tr.context_blurb:
A vacuum flask keeps coffee hot and lemonade cold because it slows heat in both directions. James Dewar, a Scottish scientist of London's Royal Institution, built the first one in 1892, and he was not thinking of picnics.

Dewar spent years forcing gases into liquid form at extremely low temperatures, and he needed a way to keep those liquefied gases cold long enough to study them. His flask had two glass walls with empty space between them, the air drawn out, and he first showed it on Christmas Day 1892.

Heat travels three ways. It can pass from molecule to molecule, or ride along in moving air or liquid; with the molecules removed from the gap, both routes are blocked. The third way, radiation, is infrared light, and it crosses a vacuum easily, so Dewar silvered the glass to reflect it back. Yet a flask of coffee still cools in the end, and most of the heat escapes at the neck, through the stopper, where the two walls must join and there is no vacuum. That is why the lid matters more than the walls.

Dewar never patented his flask; he saw it as a scientific instrument. Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner, glassblowers in Germany, made a sturdy household version in a protective case and a public contest gave it a name in 1904: "Thermos", from the Greek for heat. Dewar sued to claim the rights and lost the case outright, and the Thermos company kept the fortune.

diederik-stapel-caught-by-his-own-studen.context_blurb:
Diederik Stapel, a celebrated social psychologist at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, published eye-catching findings for years, such as the claim that litter in a station makes people more racist. His results always came out beautifully. They were invented, and he was caught not by a famous rival but by the least powerful people in his own department.

In September 2011 Stapel made world headlines with the claim that people who think about meat turn more selfish. Other researchers noticed a warning sign: the finding went out in a press release before any journal had seen the paper.

The people who caught him were three junior researchers working under him. They had noticed that he always handed them finished datasets that nobody had watched him collect, and that he discouraged questions about where the numbers came from. When they compared the files he had given them for different papers, they found identical rows of scores in two separate studies, something real data from different people cannot produce.

They took their evidence to their department head, Zeelenberg, while he was at a conference in London, so that Stapel could not be tipped off. When the university's rector asked Stapel for contacts at the Dutch schools he said had run his surveys, he admitted that no such schools existed; he had invented the data from scratch. The weakness that let it last is one anyone can spot: one person was the only source of every dataset, and no co-author ever met a participant.

The investigating committee, chaired by Willem Levelt, a psycholinguist, reported in late November 2012. It found faked or manipulated data in at least 55 of Stapel's papers, and retractions eventually reached 58. Graduate students had built doctorates on results that were never real.

dismissed-then-made-into-a-unit.context_blurb:
Ohm, Doppler and Arrhenius now live on in units, effects and a Nobel Prize, yet each was first shrugged off. The pattern is less persecution than a gap between a claim and the ability of other scientists to test it or use it, and three stories show how that gap closed.

Georg Simon Ohm, a teacher at a Cologne school, set out in an 1827 book the law relating current, voltage and resistance: double the voltage across a wire and the current doubles. His book was coldly received, no university wanted him, and he left his job; today the unit of resistance, the ohm, bears his name. Twenty-five years of minor teaching jobs followed before the University of Munich gave him a professorship of physics in 1852, less than two years before he died.

Christian Doppler argued in Prague in 1842 that motion changes the pitch we hear: an approaching source sounds higher, a retreating one lower. In the same paper he used the idea to explain why some double stars are coloured, and there he was wrong, because real stars move far too slowly to change colour that way. The sound half was tested in 1845, when the Dutch meteorologist Christophorus Buys Ballot, hoping to disprove Doppler, put a band of trumpeters on an open railway carriage near Utrecht, while trained listeners beside the track heard their note drop about a half tone as it passed. In 1848 Hippolyte Fizeau saw how to test it in light: the dark lines in a star's spectrum shift toward the red end when the star moves away from us.

Svante Arrhenius's 1884 Uppsala thesis claimed that salts dissolved in water split into charged ions by themselves, with no current needed. His examiners graded the thesis fourth class, the lowest passing mark, too low to qualify him to teach at a university. Outsiders saw its worth first: Clausius, Ostwald and van 't Hoff championed the theory, and in 1903 it won Arrhenius the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In his Nobel lecture he called Ostwald the theory's enthusiastic godfather.

dna-fingerprinting-the-morning-of-10-sep.context_blurb:
On the morning of Monday 10 September 1984, at Leicester University, the geneticist Alec Jeffreys took a freshly developed X-ray film out of its tank and found a way to tell people apart by their DNA. Within four years it had freed one innocent man and convicted a murderer, and it has kept raising hard questions ever since.

He had not been looking for an identity test. Since about 1980 he had hunted stretches of DNA that vary a lot between people, because the old markers were nearly the same in everybody and so useless for following a hereditary disease down through a family. The film was a test of whether his probe worked across species, so beside the human samples sat DNA from a cow, a grey seal and a tobacco plant. His first reaction was disgust; "what a mess," he thought. Then he looked longer, and the penny dropped.

Three lanes held the DNA of his technician, Jenny Foxon, and of her mother and father. Her pattern of bands was unlike anyone else's, yet every one of her bands could be found in one parent or the other: a personal barcode that was also a family record. The variable stretches, called minisatellites, are short sequences repeated in a row, thirty copies in one person and twenty-five in the next. Their counts change thousands of times faster than ordinary DNA because, when eggs and sperm are made, the repeats on paired chromosomes line up out of step and swap unequal lengths.

Within the hour Jeffreys and his colleague Victoria Wilson listed uses for the discovery. When he later suggested in a public talk that it might one day catch criminals, part of the audience laughed.

Its first real use was in an immigration dispute. In 1985 British officials refused entry to a fifteen-year-old, Andrew Sarbah, claiming he was an impostor. His father was out of reach, so Jeffreys rebuilt the father's pattern from the mother and three undisputed siblings, since any band in a sibling that the mother lacked must have come from the father. Andrew's bands matched, and he stayed.

Then came murder. In 1986 Leicestershire police brought Jeffreys samples from two linked killings near the village of Narborough, hoping to confirm that Richard Buckland, a seventeen-year-old who had confessed to one, had done both. The film showed that both had been committed by the same man, and that he was not Buckland, who became the first person in the world cleared by DNA. Police then wrote to every local man in the right age range asking for a blood sample, the world's first mass DNA screen. Over eight months 5,511 men gave samples, and only one refused, but there was no match. The killer, Colin Pitchfork, a cake decorator, had paid a workmate, Ian Kelly, to give blood in his place, getting him past the identity check by putting Kelly's photograph in his own passport. Kelly let it slip in a pub, and Pitchfork was arrested. In January 1988 he became the first murderer convicted through DNA, but because he pleaded guilty, no court ever examined the DNA evidence.

A DNA match is a probability, not a certainty. Its number states how uncommon the matching pattern is among the people it is checked against, which is why careful accounts give Pitchfork's odds as anything from one in ten million to one in 700 million. Sensitive modern tests bring new risks. In 2012 Lukis Anderson was charged with a murder in California because traces of his DNA turned up beneath the dead man's nails, though he had spent the night in hospital; the paramedics who had treated him earlier that day had answered the murder call and carried his cells there. By 2009 Britain's DNA database held profiles of some 800,000 people arrested but never charged. Jeffreys protested that his genome was his property, not the state's, and after a European court ruled the retention unlawful, most of those profiles were destroyed. DNA has also exposed how weak other evidence can be: of 375 Americans freed by DNA after conviction, 29 percent had confessed or incriminated themselves.

dna-the-evidence-darwin-never-had.context_blurb:
Charles Darwin argued in 1859 that all living things share ancestors, but he had no idea how heredity worked, and the strongest evidence for his idea arrived long after his death. It came from DNA and proteins, along several lines that could have contradicted one another and did not.

The code of life is shared, and that is useful. Before 1982, insulin for diabetics was extracted from slaughterhouse animals. In August 1978 David Goeddel's team at Genentech announced that it had made real human insulin in the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli, by giving it synthetic human genes for the hormone's two chains. A bacterium can read a human gene because all life uses the same genetic code.

Scurvy offers another clue. For a century researchers could not give the disease to lab animals, because rats, mice and dogs make their own vitamin C. Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich succeeded in 1907 with the guinea pig, which cannot, and that animal later let Albert Szent-Györgyi isolate vitamin C in 1928. Humans cannot make vitamin C either, yet the gene for the last enzyme in the pathway is still in our DNA, wrecked, a broken pseudogene called GULOP. The ability broke in an ancestor of monkeys, apes and us about 63 million years ago. Lemurs and lorises belong to a primate branch that split off before the break, and they still make their own.

Proteins tell the same story. Cytochrome c, a small protein that passes electrons along inside every breathing cell, is about 104 amino acids long. The human and chimpanzee versions differ at none of those positions, a rhesus monkey's at one and baker's yeast's at 44. The order of those differences matches the family tree built from bones. The protein is also interchangeable: human cytochrome oxidase, its working partner, accepted the cytochrome c of wheat, and so did every other pairing of species tested.

Our genomes carry fossil viruses. A retrovirus pastes its genes into the DNA of the cell it infects, and when it hits a sperm or egg the insert is inherited forever. Some 98,000 such elements and fragments make up roughly five to eight percent of human DNA. Almost all are dead wreckage, but one viral gene, which a virus uses to fuse itself into cells, now makes proteins called syncytins that fuse cells into the layer of the placenta that feeds and shields a growing baby. Shared inserts at the same address in related species point to a shared ancestor, and a missing one can be checked too. M. Barbulescu's team reported in 2001 on a HERV-K insert present in chimpanzees, bonobos and gorillas but absent in humans, whose DNA at that address is untouched.

Our chromosomes record a merger. Humans have 23 pairs; chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans have 24. J. W. IJdo's team found in 1991, in the middle of human chromosome 2, telomere repeats, the caps that normally sit only at a chromosome's ends, running head to head where two ancestral chromosomes had fused. The boldest test came in 2015, when Kachroo, Marcotte and colleagues knocked out 414 essential yeast genes one at a time and swapped in the matching human gene. Close to half of the human versions let the yeast survive, across about a billion years of separation.

Darwin's own gap was heredity. In 1867 the engineer Fleeming Jenkin argued that if offspring come out midway between their parents, a rare helpful variation is halved in each generation until it is diluted away before selection can use it; Darwin said Jenkin had helped him more than any other critic. The answer was already in print. Gregor Mendel, a friar in Brünn, had shown with pea plants that inheritance runs on separate, stable factors, but his 1866 paper sat unread for a generation, until three botanists independently found it in 1900.

One caution. Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling proposed in 1962 that protein changes accumulate at a fairly regular pace, a molecular clock. Even a perfect clock would have a limit: molecular differences on their own give only a count of changes, never an absolute date, so the clock must be calibrated against independent evidence such as fossils.

e-mc2-the-smallest-number-with-the-bigge.context_blurb:
E = mc² says that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, and that a tiny loss of mass releases an enormous amount of energy. It explains why the Sun shines, and at Christmas 1938 it let two exiles in the Swedish snow work out what had happened inside a split uranium atom.

Every second the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and the helium weighs about 4 million tonnes less. That missing mass leaves the Sun as sunlight. Before fusion was known, Kelvin and Helmholtz had argued that the Sun shines by slowly shrinking, which would keep it going for about 100 million years. Geology killed the idea: rocks laid down in liquid water some 4 billion years ago demanded a far older Sun.

On 19 December 1938 the chemist Otto Hahn sent a letter from Berlin to his old partner Lise Meitner. He and Fritz Strassmann had bombarded uranium with neutrons, and something that came out behaved like barium, which was impossible because barium is barely half as heavy as uranium. The nucleus had not been chipped; it had split near the middle. Meitner, driven out of Germany that summer, was spending Christmas in Sweden, and with her nephew Otto Frisch she worked it out during a walk in the snow, sitting on a tree trunk and writing on scraps of paper. The two fragments weighed less than the uranium nucleus by about a fifth of a proton's mass, and E = mc² turned that into about 200 million electron-volts for every split. In Copenhagen, Frisch took a word from a biologist colleague for the process: fission, the word for a living cell dividing into two.

Frisch then checked the arithmetic with an instrument. His uranium sample also threw out millions of alpha particles, so he set his detector's threshold above the size of any alpha pulse, high enough that only a split could clear it; on 13 January 1939 the big pulses came through. Yet the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering fission went to Otto Hahn alone, naming neither Meitner, who explained it, nor Frisch, who measured it.

The equation had already passed a test at the bench. Cockcroft and Walton split lithium with protons in 1932, and the masses needed to check E = mc² came from Francis Aston's mass spectrograph: the predicted energy and the measured one agreed to within about half a percent.

Chemistry loses mass too, only far less. Fission a tonne of uranium-235 and about a kilogram vanishes as energy, but a thousand tonnes of burned coal loses only about half a gram, far too little for any balance to catch. Why do fusion and fission both release energy? How tightly a nucleus holds each of its particles rises with size, peaks at iron-56 and then falls, so joining light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both move toward that peak. The most complete conversion of all happens in hospital PET scanners: when a positron meets an electron, both vanish into two photons of exactly 511 thousand electron-volts, the electron's mass expressed as energy.

earthrise-the-photograph-that-was-not-on.context_blurb:
The most famous photograph of Earth was not in the flight plan. On Christmas Eve 1968 Apollo 8, the first mission to carry people to the Moon, was on its fourth orbit with its cameras aimed at the lunar surface for a mapping run, when Earth came up over the Moon's horizon. Bill Anders, the mission photographer, grabbed a fresh roll of colour film.

Earth seemed to climb above a still horizon, but neither Earth nor the Moon was doing the moving. The Moon turns far too slowly to lift Earth into view in seconds; what carried Earth across the window was the command module's own motion along its orbit and its changing attitude. From a fixed spot on the Moon's near side, Earth never rises at all.

For fifty years most books said the commander, Frank Borman, took a first black-and-white frame before Anders found colour film. In 2018 Ernie Wright, a visualiser at NASA Goddard, matched the cockpit voice recording against the spacecraft's recorded movements and showed that every one of the three frames was Anders's; Borman accepted the correction. The famous print was also adjusted before release. Anders saw the lunar horizon running down the side of the frame, and NASA and the press turned the picture about 90 degrees clockwise to give it the look of a sunrise.

eclipses-predicted-to-the-minute.context_blurb:
A total eclipse of the Sun happens somewhere on Earth about every eighteen months, but its shadow crosses only a narrow strip, so any one town may wait centuries. Ancient astronomers learned to predict when eclipses would return long before anyone could explain why.

Why not every month? The Moon passes between Earth and the Sun at each new moon, about every 29.5 days, but its orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to the path the Sun seems to follow across our sky, so usually it slides just above or below the Sun. Only a new moon near one of the two crossing points can cast its shadow on Earth.

Babylonian astronomers, combing centuries of eclipse records on clay tablets, found a rhythm now called the saros: eighteen years, eleven days and eight hours, after which the Sun, Earth and Moon return to nearly the same arrangement and a similar eclipse repeats. The extra eight hours is a third of a day, so Earth has turned an extra third of a spin, and each eclipse in the series falls about a third of the way around the world to the west. Only after three saroses, about 54 years, does the shadow come back near the same longitude.

Total eclipses depend on a lucky match: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost the same size in our sky. When the Moon is at the far end of its orbit it looks slightly too small, and the eclipse leaves a bright ring. The match will not last. Reflectors left by three Apollo crews let observatories time laser pulses to the Moon and back, and the record shows it moving away by about 3.8 centimetres a year, so one day it will look too small ever to cover the Sun completely.

eddingtons-eclipse-the-test-that-made-ei.context_blurb:
When the Sun went dark on 29 May 1919, British expeditions were waiting with cameras to test Albert Einstein's new theory of gravity, and the result made Einstein world-famous overnight. The full story is messier and more honest than the legend: the leader was nearly jailed, the best camera failed, and a charge of bias was answered sixty years later.

Arthur Eddington, a Cambridge astronomer, was a Quaker who refused to fight in the First World War. In July 1918 a tribunal was about to send him to a labour camp, but the Astronomer Royal, Frank Dyson, persuaded it to let him go free on condition that he led the British eclipse expedition of 1919. So the pacifist who would not fight Germans went to test a German's theory. On the African island of Principe his only helper was Edwin Cottingham, a clockmaker, there to keep the clock drives running so the telescopes tracked the sky.

There were three possible answers. Light untouched by gravity would not bend at all. Light treated as tiny particles falling under Newton's gravity would bend by 0.87 of a second of arc at the Sun's edge, and that was exactly the figure Einstein himself had published in 1911, before his theory was finished: it was Newton's own answer. His completed theory of November 1915 doubled it to 1.75. Einstein had been lucky. In 1914 the young Berlin astronomer Erwin Finlay-Freundlich set off to measure the bend at an eclipse, with money Einstein had raised from the arms magnate Gustav Krupp, but war broke out, Freundlich was interned and his instruments seized. A successful 1914 measurement would have contradicted Einstein's prediction of the time.

Dyson had chosen the date with care. To catch a shift smaller than two arcseconds you need many bright stars close beside the hidden Sun, and on 29 May 1919 the Sun stood among the Hyades, a rich star cluster in Taurus. The method compared two photographs of the same stars: one taken during totality, the other at a time when the Sun stood far off in another part of the sky. Light passing the Sun bends toward it, so on the eclipse plates each star appeared pushed outward, away from the centre of the Sun, most strongly for stars nearest its edge.

The other team went to Sobral in Brazil. As the morning heated up, the steel tube of its main telescope stretched, the focus drifted and the stars came out as smudges. The number that won came instead from a small 4-inch lens lent by a Jesuit astronomer, Father Aloysius Cortie, almost as an afterthought: 1.98 seconds of arc, against 1.61 from Principe. Both sat near Einstein's value and far from Newton's, though the error bars were large. Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin stayed in Brazil until late July so that they could photograph the same star field at night with the same telescope on the same spot, letting any distortion of the instrument appear in both sets of plates and cancel out.

The value was really pinned down in 1922. At Wallal in Western Australia, under a cloudless sky, William Campbell's party from Lick Observatory, led by a man who had doubted relativity, photographed more than a hundred stars and measured 1.72 seconds of arc. Today no eclipse is needed: radio telescopes track distant quasars as the Sun passes near them in the sky, and they confirm the bend to a small fraction of a percent.

The philosophers John Earman and Clark Glymour accused the 1919 team, in 1980, of bias: the one set of plates that came out near Newton's value, the smeared Sobral set, had been discarded. The answer came from the evidence itself. In 1979 Geoffrey Harvey and E. D. Clements had re-measured the original plates with a modern machine, and the discarded set came out at 1.55 seconds of arc, no longer favouring Newton; it had been dropped for a real instrument fault. And the historian Daniel Kennefick found that the Sobral notebooks are in Frank Dyson's handwriting, not Eddington's, and that Eddington learned the Sobral numbers by letter. Dyson, the sceptic, had expected a different result.

einsteins-lens-the-effect-he-said-we-wou.context_blurb:
Einstein's theory says gravity bends light, so a massive object can act as a lens, bending the light of something far behind it into a ring or a double image. Einstein himself thought it would never be seen.

In 1936 he published a short note on the idea in the journal Science, only because a Czech engineer, Rudi Mandl, kept pestering him, and concluded that a visible lining-up of two stars was so improbable that no one would ever observe it. A year later Fritz Zwicky, a Swiss-American astronomer at Caltech, replied that Einstein had missed the obvious: entire galaxies, which Zwicky called extragalactic nebulae, would make far better lenses, and measuring their bending would let astronomers weigh them, including mass that gives no light.

The idea waited forty years. At Kitt Peak in 1979, Dennis Walsh and his colleagues Robert Carswell and Ray Weymann examined a close pair of quasars. Their light had essentially identical spectra and matching redshifts, which two separate quasars would never share: it was one quasar seen twice, its light split around a giant galaxy in between. Today astronomers use the same trick to map dark matter.

einsteins-packets-and-the-man-who-spent-.context_blurb:
Shine dim blue light on certain metals and electrons fly out at once; shine bright red light and none do. This photoelectric effect broke the wave theory of light, led Einstein to propose that light comes in packets, and drove one American physicist to spend ten years trying to prove him wrong.

Heinrich Hertz stumbled on it in 1887 at Karlsruhe while proving that Maxwell's electromagnetic waves were real. When light from his first spark fell on the metal knobs of a second spark gap, the second spark jumped across far more easily. Hertz noted it and moved on. In 1888 Wilhelm Hallwachs charged a clean zinc plate negatively, connected to a gold-leaf electroscope with its leaves spread apart, and shone ultraviolet light on it: the leaves fell together as the charge drained away. Light was knocking negative charge out of the metal, a test a school can still run.

In 1902 Philipp Lenard measured the escaping electrons with a reverse voltage that turned back the fastest ones. When he made his lamp brighter, more electrons escaped, but the fastest of them went no faster; only the colour of the light changed that. A wave should do the opposite. Lenard explained it with a trigger: the light only released energy already sitting inside the atom, like a fuse firing a loaded gun, and most physicists accepted that until about 1911. The wave picture also predicted a delay while an electron soaked up energy from faint light, but even with the dimmest lamps electrons flew out immediately, and no delay has ever been measured.

Writing to his friend Conrad Habicht in May 1905, Einstein described the four papers of his remarkable year and called only one of them very revolutionary: not relativity, but the paper on radiation and light. In it he proposed that light's energy is not spread smoothly but arrives in countable packets, each absorbed whole by a single electron. A packet of blue light carries enough energy to free an electron, a packet of red light does not, and a brighter lamp sends more packets, never bigger ones.

Robert Millikan, famous for measuring the electron's charge, expected the equation to fail and spent ten years testing it. Alkali metals tarnish the instant air touches them, so he built what he called a machine shop in a vacuum, shaving fresh metal with a knife worked by a magnet, all inside a quartz tube, because ordinary glass absorbs the ultraviolet light he needed. He plotted the stopping voltage against the frequency of the light and got a straight line, and its slope gave him Planck's constant to about half a percent, the same number Max Planck had found from a completely different phenomenon. Yet in the January 1916 paper confirming the equation, Millikan still wrote that the theory behind it seemed at present wholly untenable. He accepted the equation and rejected the picture.

What finally won physicists over came in 1923. Arthur Compton bounced X-rays off graphite and found a second scattered line whose wavelength was longer than the original, and longer the wider the scattering angle: exactly what happens if each X-ray packet hits an electron like a billiard ball and loses energy to it. Bohr, Kramers and Slater tried once more in 1924 to save the wave picture, and paid a huge price: they let the conservation of energy fail in single collisions and hold only on average. In 1925 Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger timed scattered X-rays and recoiling electrons together and found them firing in step, as conservation in every collision demands. Bohr gave his theory, as he put it, an honourable funeral.

el-nino-catching-the-pacific-in-the-act.context_blurb:
El Niño, the periodic warming of the eastern Pacific, shapes weather around the world. It was pieced together from two separate clues: a failed Indian monsoon studied with pencil and paper, and a warm current known to Peruvian fishermen for centuries.

In 1877 the Indian summer monsoon almost completely failed. Crops withered and wells ran dry across southern India, and the Great Famine, which ran from 1876 into 1878, killed more than ten million people; British relief policy made it worse. The disaster drove the colonial government to seek a way to forecast the monsoon.

In 1904 the British sent out a Cambridge mathematician, Gilbert Walker, who had worked on electromagnetism and spinning tops but never on weather. He set a room of Indian clerks computing by hand which places' weather rose and fell together, and over some twenty years they found a see-saw in air pressure across the whole Pacific. When pressure at Tahiti is high, pressure at Darwin, in Australia, is low, and then the reverse; Walker named it the Southern Oscillation. He could describe it in fine detail but never explain it, and most meteorologists dismissed it as a statistical curiosity.

Meanwhile the fishermen of Peru had for generations known a warm current that arrived every few years around Christmas, drove off the cold-water anchovies and ruined the fishing. They called it El Niño, the Christ Child, after the season it came.

Normally the trade winds blow from east to west along the equator and pile warm surface water toward Indonesia, holding the sea there about half a metre higher than off Peru, while cold, nutrient-rich water wells up along the South American coast. Jacob Bjerknes, a Norwegian-American meteorologist, put the two mysteries together in 1969: the pressure see-saw and the warm current are one coupled system, in which the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other. The loop runs away on its own. When the trade winds slacken, warm water slides east; the warmer eastern sea then weakens the winds still further. That feedback is why the Pacific flips between states instead of drifting.

teaches.1dbaca39d6: Crops withered and wells ran dry across southern India, and the Great Famine, which ran from 1876 into 1878, killed more than ten million people; British relief policy made it worse.
teaches.941bd89c88: He set a room of Indian clerks computing by hand which places' weather rose and fell together, and over some twenty years they found a see-saw in air pressure across the whole Pacific.
teaches.6c7425705b: When pressure at Tahiti is high, pressure at Darwin, in Australia, is low, and then the reverse; Walker named it the Southern Oscillation.
teaches.8d74895d52: They called it El Niño, the Christ Child, after the season it came.
teaches.267bc66f0b: Normally the trade winds blow from east to west along the equator and pile warm surface water toward Indonesia, holding the sea there about half a metre higher than off Peru, while cold, nutrient-rich water wells up along the South American coast.
teaches.16d8732f47: Jacob Bjerknes, a Norwegian-American meteorologist, put the two mysteries together in 1969: the pressure see-saw and the warm current are one coupled system, in which the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other.
teaches.43f307fe32: When the trade winds slacken, warm water slides east; the warmer eastern sea then weakens the winds still further.

emily-rosa-aged-eleven-in-a-medical-jour.context_blurb: A fourth-grader's science fair project tested a claim no adult had bothered to test. Nine-year-old Emily Rosa sat practitioners of a popular therapy at a table with a cardboard screen between them, had them push their hands through two holes, flipped a coin to decide left or right, and asked them to perform the specific perceptual task the therapy claimed. The entire apparatus was a screen and a coin, and the entire scientific move was to strip away every cue except the one being claimed, the same move as the blindfold Benjamin Franklin's commission put on Mesmer's patients, and the blinders eventually put on the horse Clever Hans. The therapy being tested, Therapeutic Touch, was taught at the time in nursing schools; practitioners said they could sense and smooth a human energy field with their hands without touching the patient.

emily-whiteheads-rewired-t-cells.context_blurb: The first child in the world treated with the therapy was a six-year-old from Pennsylvania whose leukemia had come back twice and whose chemotherapy had stopped working. In 2012, doctors at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia drew out a specific population of her immune cells, rewired them in the lab to recognise a protein found on the surface of her cancer cells, and put them back to hunt. The genetic cargo that gave them their new recognition was carried in by a stripped-down virus whose everyday identity most people would find alarming on a hospital consent form, kept only for its one real talent, splicing a new instruction permanently into a chromosome. Days after infusion the child's fever spiked and she went onto a ventilator in intensive care, because the engineered cells were doing their job so violently that the body's own signalling system had locked into a crisis loop. The team identified the key signalling molecule, measured its runaway concentration, and reached for a drug already licensed for an entirely different disease, an existing arthritis antibody that happened to block exactly the receptor involved. She came back. Her bone marrow soon showed no detectable cancer. In August 2017 the US regulator approved the therapy as the first treatment including a gene-therapy step ever cleared in the United States. The drug wipes out healthy cells too, so many patients need lifelong replacement, and this approach has transformed blood cancers while largely failing so far against solid ones.

entropy-and-the-arrow-of-time.context_blurb: Scrambling an egg is easy; unscrambling it never happens, even though nothing in the laws of motion forbids the reverse, run every collision backwards and each one is still legal. What stops time running the wrong way is not a law of force but a matter of overwhelming odds. A shuffled deck is not messy, it is one of an astronomically larger family than the sorted one, which is why shuffling looks irreversible. Rudolf Clausius coined the word in 1865 from Greek roots, deliberately making it sound like 'energy' because the two quantities travel together. The arrow pointing forward because the early universe was in an extraordinarily low-entropy state is a fact, but why it was that way is not explained. The thermodynamic end-of-everything prediction extends classical reasoning in a direction physicists increasingly argue is not well defined when gravity and cosmic expansion dominate.

epigenetics-and-the-dutch-hunger-winter.context_blurb: Marks written on top of the genetic code, how far they reach, and how far they do not. A calico or tortoiseshell cat is a walking demonstration of gene silencing, with early random decisions in individual cells carried forward in every daughter cell. A chemical tag added to a specific base can silence a gene without altering a single letter of the sequence, and the tag is copied when a cell divides, so the pattern is inherited within the body. A controlled demonstration in agouti mice showed that a diet rich in specific methyl donors during pregnancy could flip a coat colour and metabolic trait in the pups, without changing a single sequence letter. The human case is a tragic natural experiment, the German-blockaded western Netherlands in the last winter of the war, with precise ration records continuing through the famine, which produced one of the best-documented cohorts in human biology. In mammals, the germ line wipes most of these marks twice, and the human evidence for true transgenerational transmission to grandchildren and beyond is thin, indirect and confounded.

eratosthenes-stick-and-the-size-of-the-e.context_blurb: Around 240 BC a scholar in Alexandria had a report from an upriver town: at noon on a specific day of the year the Sun stood exactly overhead there, and no vertical rod cast a shadow at all. On that same noon far to the north a rod in Alexandria DID cast a shadow, and he measured its angle. From a geometry so simple a child can follow it, he computed the fraction of a full circle between the two sites, multiplied by the known distance between them, and read off a figure for the circumference of the Earth. The distance figure itself had not come from a surveyor's chain. Nobody today knows for certain which unit of length he was using, so the only truthful claim is 'within a few percent, depending on the choice'. Later estimates by a rival shrank the Earth, and that undersized version was the one Columbus leaned on when he argued Asia was reachable by sailing west. The scholar's own book on the measurement is lost; the method survives only through a later textbook.

every-raindrop-is-signed.context_blurb: Lighter water evaporates slightly more readily and heavier water condenses slightly more readily, so every evaporation and every rainfall sorts the two. A Danish scientist in the early 1950s set collectors through a two-day rainstorm and found the ratio tracked a specific atmospheric variable, a liquid thermometer, in effect. The chemist who had discovered deuterium realised the same sorting is locked into carbonate as it crystallises, so a dead shell records conditions at the time of its growth. In 1961 the ratios in rain and snow from all over the world fell on a single global line. Isotopes in human tissue carry the signature of where a person grew up. The deepest ice cores reach hundreds of thousands of years, and the bubbles trapped in them turn out not to be proxies at all but actual preserved samples of ancient air. A Pleistocene temperature record once read as pure thermometer was later recognised to also encode a different variable, which made the method more useful, not less. And a nuclear-weapons scar was turned into a dating tool used today.

falling-around-the-world-why-astronauts-.context_blurb: At the International Space Station's altitude, Earth's gravity is still a surprisingly large fraction of its value on your kitchen floor, nowhere near zero, nowhere near 'escape'. Astronauts float because the station and everyone in it are in free fall together: the astronaut, the wall and the floating pen all accelerate toward Earth at the same rate, so nothing presses on anything. Newton's own illustration of the point, from A Treatise of the System of the World, is a cannon on a mountaintop firing horizontally, faster and faster, until the ground curves away beneath the shot as fast as the shot drops, so it never lands. That is an orbit. Orbit is simply free fall that does not end.

faraday-the-bookbinders-apprentice.context_blurb: The greatest experimentalist of the nineteenth century had almost no schooling, almost no mathematics, and almost no business being in a laboratory at all. A London bookbinder's apprentice taught himself science while serving his trade. At twenty he attended Humphry Davy's lectures, wrote up his notes in careful detail, and made a specific personal effort with those notes that got him hired. From there he produced some of the most consequential experiments in modern physics with instruments he could build on a bench. He made a current-carrying wire pivot continuously around a magnet in mercury, an early device turning electricity into motion for the first time, and, a decade later, discovered the law of electromagnetic induction, with its surprising detail about when a galvanometer's needle actually moves. He built a famous caged room to test an idea about where charge actually sits on a conductor. He had no calculus; his tool was a particular diagrammatic language of forces through empty space, and Maxwell later turned those drawings into equations. A famous one-line retort to a politician, often cited in textbooks, cannot in fact be found anywhere Faraday or his contemporaries wrote it, and the usual attribution does not survive a careful check. He refused the Royal Society presidency twice, refused a knighthood, and preferred to stay plain Mr Faraday.

faradays-candle-a-whole-course-hiding-in.context_blurb: Six Royal Institution Christmas Lectures delivered to a juvenile audience on a single burning candle are the most famous science lectures ever given. Faraday's claim was that there is no better door into the whole of natural philosophy than the chemistry of a flame; the lectures became a book edited from his words in the early 1860s by someone else. The wax is the fuel but nothing solid actually burns; a specific mechanism carries melted wax up the wick before anything is lit. The neat shaped cup at the top of a candle is held in place by a specific effect of the draught, not by the wax's structure. The yellow of the flame is not a glowing gas at all. The flame is hollow inside, and Faraday drew the unburned vapour off through a bent tube and lit it at the far end. A candle makes water, and he decomposed that water back into its two gases on the lecture bench. He closed the course by comparing respiration itself to the same chemistry run slow, a child and a flame both taking in oxygen and giving back carbonic acid, differing only in speed and temperature. In microgravity, a candle flame is a small sphere rather than the teardrop everyone draws.

fever-is-a-weapon-not-a-malfunction.context_blurb: In 1975 three researchers infected desert iguanas with a bacterium, then arranged their enclosures so the animals could choose how warm they wanted to be. A lizard cannot heat itself from the inside; it has to go and find heat, which is precisely what makes it the right animal for this experiment. The infected lizards took a specific thermoregulatory action and pushed their body temperature up, and the ones allowed to do so survived far better than the ones kept cool. The paper came out in Science that April, with the plain title 'Fever and survival'. The reptile IS the experiment. In a mammal you cannot separate the fever from the infection that produced it, because they arrive together. In a cold-blooded animal you can. Fever is not the infection overheating you; it is your own hypothalamus deliberately moving its target, driven by specific molecules in the brain. That is why you feel freezing cold while your temperature is climbing, the chill is the ascent to the new setting, not the illness. Whether suppressing fever helps or hurts in critically ill patients is unsettled, with mixed trial evidence. What is settled is that the thermostat has not broken.

feynman-the-o-ring-and-the-glass-of-ice-.context_blurb: One simple demonstration cut through months of bureaucratic analysis. During a live televised hearing of the Rogers Commission in February 1986, Richard Feynman produced a scrap from a part of the shuttle booster, squeezed it flat in a C-clamp, dropped it in the glass of ice water sitting on the witness table, fished it out and showed what it did when released. The specific job of the part being tested was to spring back instantly when a joint flexed at ignition, and the morning of the launch had been colder than any previous launch by a wide margin. The night before, the booster contractor's engineers had argued against going; the company's no-launch recommendation was reversed before morning. Feynman had been pointed at the cold by a US Air Force general on the commission, who had passed on test data a quieter informant had given him. He insisted a dissenting appendix be included, whose closing line about honesty is one of the most-quoted sentences in American engineering. A sociologist later gave the institutional failure a name the whole engineering world has adopted.

feynmans-cargo-cult-science.context_blurb: The 1974 Caltech commencement address that gave scientific self-deception a name and an image. Feynman described South Sea islanders who, after the war, built the FORM of an airfield, runways with fires along the sides, a wooden hut, a man sitting in it with two wooden pieces on his head like headphones and bars of bamboo sticking out like antennas, and waited for the planes. 'The form is perfect,' he said; it just doesn't work. The first principle, which Feynman stated as a single sentence that names the hardest form of self-deception. The 'Millikan creep', a classic case of an error-of-friendship across decades, where measurements of a famous value crept slowly toward the truth after the first paper rather than jumping, and Feynman's diagnosis that this is a story about honest people, not fraud. A rat-maze experiment in which almost nobody repeated the one control the original researcher had proved was necessary. Feynman's own phrase for the standard of integrity he was asking of his audience, and the honest-advertising counter-example from a cooking-oil ad. The islanders' religious movements were and are real, not a Feynman invention.

flame-tests-the-fingerprint-in-the-fire.context_blurb: A colour turned out to be a name. The German chemist Robert Bunsen designed the eponymous laboratory burner specifically to solve a flame problem, an ordinary gas lamp was too sooty and too yellow to let him see what was really happening, and he needed a nearly colourless flame as a background. Then he and the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff put a prism between the flame and the eye, which turned a smear of colour into a sharp set of lines, and the same element produced the same lines every time. In 1860, boiled down from mineral spring water, a set of lines appeared that belonged to no catalogued element; another appeared in the same water the following year. Both were later shown to exist on Earth, but neither had ever been held before someone saw them in a flame. Kirchhoff later matched his bright laboratory lines against the dark lines Fraunhofer had charted in sunlight in 1814, overthrowing in the process a confident impossibility declared by a famous philosopher in the 1830s.

flemings-open-dish-and-the-forgotten-hal.context_blurb: The most famous accident in medicine, told in full. Fleming came back from a holiday in September 1928, found a stack of forgotten culture plates, and on one of them a stray mould had grown surrounded by a ring where the bacteria were gone. He grew the mould in broth and showed the filtered liquid still killed the bacteria at high dilution, the killer was a substance the mould was leaking, not the mould itself, and he named the substance in a 1929 paper. The paper went into a specialist journal with the stuff pitched mainly as a laboratory curiosity, because he could not purify it, could not keep it from falling apart within days, and could not cure anybody with it. Almost nobody chased it for a decade. The real story shifts to Oxford in 1940 and to Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley, whose work converted a sticky substance into a drug. A famous overnight mouse experiment made it a medicine. The world hunt for a better strain ended in a fruit market in Peoria, Illinois. By 1944 industrial output was staggering. The 1945 Nobel went to three men only, and the technician whose extraction made the mouse experiment possible got nothing.

flemings-tears-the-bodys-own-antiseptic.context_blurb: Alexander Fleming's 1921 discovery of a natural antibacterial substance started with a specific bodily fluid landing on a culture plate while he had a cold, and a zone around the drop clearing to jelly. The human body was manufacturing a germ-killer on its own, and a drop of one had just landed on his plate by accident. He hunted for the substance everywhere he thought it might be concealed in nature, from secretions he could collect himself to everyday animal products, named both the substance and the test organism in Greek, and then, crucially, did not succeed in turning any of it into a medicine. The reason sits in the mechanism he eventually worked out: the compound dissolves the sugar wall of exactly the wrong group of bacteria for a drug, which is why Fleming could never make it clinically useful. The compound is a real defence found in tears, saliva and other secretions, and it is NOT why most of us do not get infections.

float-a-steel-paperclip-then-touch-it-wi.context_blurb: A steel paperclip is nearly eight times denser than water and has no business floating. Water acts as if it has a thin, stretchable skin, and the skin is strong enough to hold a flat piece of metal that logically should sink. Soap destroys that skin by inserting itself into it, which is why water with soap in it wets things that bead water off, and why one drop in a plate of peppered water sends the pepper to the rim. Agnes Pockels poured oil films on water, measured when the surface tension suddenly changed, and from that derived how much room one molecule took up. A paperclip is held by the top layer of the liquid, which the soap wrecks.

fluorescence-light-that-comes-back-chang.context_blurb: Some materials swallow light you cannot see and hand back light you can. In 1852 at Cambridge, a British physicist shone sunlight through a filter onto a solution of quinine and watched a specific eerie glow appear right at the surface where the beam entered. He named the effect after a mineral that does the same thing, and he stated a general rule: whatever comes out always has less energy per particle than what went in. The rule is why an ultraviolet lamp can make things glow visibly but a red lamp cannot make them glow blue. Glow-in-the-dark toys do not demonstrate the same effect. They demonstrate a longer-lived, slower cousin whose clock runs in minutes to hours rather than nanoseconds, and the toys are not 'storing light' in any ordinary sense. Scorpions glow under ultraviolet light and nobody knows why. Proposals exist; none is established.

follow-the-science-versus-the-dissent-tr.context_blurb: Ignaz Semmelweis cut childbed-fever deaths in his Vienna ward by making doctors wash in chlorinated lime, and lost his post and his career for it. Alfred Wegener showed in 1912 that the continents had moved, and geologists rejected the claim for fifty years for a reason, he could not name a specific thing his idea needed. The objection was legitimate; the ridicule was not. In 1984 Barry Marshall could not get anyone to believe bacteria caused ulcers, and so he performed a specific first-person act of persuasion. Most dissenters are simply wrong, and being mocked is not evidence that one is right; Lysenko was a 'dissenter' against Mendelian genetics. It is a tradition, not a reward system.

foucaults-pendulum-walk-in-and-watch-the.context_blurb: The first time anyone could literally see the Earth rotate was in Paris in 1851, when Leon Foucault invited the scientists of the city to come and watch a long pendulum swing. Before that date the planet's rotation was a thing inferred from astronomy; afterwards it was a thing you walked into a hall to witness. The mechanism is counter-intuitive: the pendulum is not turning. It keeps swinging in the same plane in space, and the floor, the building, Paris and the planet rotate underneath it. The rate depends on where on Earth you are. At the poles the plane completes a full circle in 24 hours; at Paris it takes about 32 hours; at the equator it never turns at all. The effect is real but overwhelmingly swamped by drain shape and leftover swirl at sink scale, as a careful 1962 experiment showed.

frances-kelsey-says-no.context_blurb: In September 1960 a brand-new medical officer took her first assignment at the US Food and Drug Administration, an application to sell a sedative already on sale across Europe, handed to Frances Kelsey as an easy one. She refused to approve the application for over a year, under heavy pressure, while the company's representatives escalated to her superiors and asked that the file be taken away from her. A medical journal letter at the end of 1960 described numbness and tingling in long-term users, which Kelsey read as evidence that the drug could reach adult nerves and therefore might reach a developing baby. She refused to accept the company's assertion that the drug did not cross the placenta, in part because her own earlier laboratory work had already shown effects she could not easily dismiss. The epidemic that eventually linked the drug to a specific congenital pattern of injuries emerged in Germany and Australia late in 1961, and the US application was withdrawn in early 1962. Congress answered with a sweeping amendment to drug law. This is a story about demanding evidence, not about reflexive opposition.

franklins-kite-and-the-rod-that-actually.context_blurb: Lightning is electricity, and the dangerous test was not the famous one. The kite was not struck by lightning. A direct strike would almost certainly have killed him. The cloud overhead induced charge on the wet string, and Franklin, sheltered in a shed, drew a spark from a key into a Leyden jar through an insulating link kept dry. Franklin was not the first person to perform his own idea; he had published the design, an insulated enclosure on a high tower with a pointed iron rod, in 1749-50, and a French natural philosopher built it near Paris in 1752 and drew sparks a month before the kite. The proposal travelled faster than the proposer. The applied test that actually worked, a pointed rod bonded to a thick conductor running all the way to damp earth, is what we have today. The rod is unquestionably his and unquestionably worked.

fraunhofers-dark-lines-and-the-philosoph.context_blurb: How a barcode in sunlight answered a question a famous philosopher had declared permanently unanswerable. The accident made the career. In 1814, testing his own world-class glass, Fraunhofer built a prism-and-telescope spectroscope, pointed it at the Sun and found that the solar spectrum is not a smooth rainbow at all but is cut by a huge number of a specific feature, which he mapped and labelled. He could not explain them. In Heidelberg in 1859-60, a near-colourless gas flame let a chemist burn a sample without the flame's own light drowning the result; Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff found each element gives its own fixed set of bright lines. From there the inversion that explains Fraunhofer: send white light through a cooler gas and the same lines come back dark. Within two years the method found elements no one had ever seen. In 1835 Auguste Comte had chosen a specific question about the stars as his standard example of knowledge forever beyond human reach, and within roughly 25 years the question had become a school laboratory exercise. Fraunhofer died at 39; his epitaph reads, in Latin, that he brought the stars nearer.

from-einsteins-spooky-action-to-the-2022.context_blurb: Make two particles together, carry one to one city and one to another, and measuring the first appears to fix what the second will say, instantly. In 1935 a famous paper argued that if you can predict the distant particle's value with certainty without touching it, that value must have been real all along, so the quantum formalism must be incomplete and the particles must be carrying hidden instructions, like twins leaving home with sealed envelopes. For twenty-nine years the question looked like a matter of taste. Then John Stewart Bell, an accelerator physicist doing foundations as a hobby, published in 1964 a theorem that turned the dispute into a test: any sealed-envelope theory must obey a specific inequality, and the formalism predicts breaking it under specific conditions. Taste became arithmetic. In 2018 the detector settings were randomised using properties of light from distant quasars whose photons had left billions of years ago. In 2022 three physicists shared the Nobel Prize. This does not permit faster-than-light communication, because each side's data alone looks like random noise and the correlation only shows up when the two lists are brought back together.

from-willow-bark-to-the-pill-in-the-cupb.context_blurb: The commonest tablet in the house, traced back to a chewed twig.
